hypotheses.statement: The entire cluster is remediation backlog from a single discrete high-wind/storm event on 2025-03-14, so the elevated rate is a one-off event signature rather than an ongoing failure process at Sundowner Mesa.

The daily/weekly count decays monotonically after mid-March and returns to fleet-baseline levels within roughly 60-90 days of the event, with no new arrivals in May-June.
Multiple narratives reference the same event vocabulary ('wind event on March 14th', 'post event walkdown', 'storm damage') and/or the same property claim reference NRS-PL-2025-0417.
Damage is spatially clustered (west side / west two-thirds of zones, per WO-2025-00214 and WO-2025-00387) rather than uniformly distributed across blocks B01-B09.

Existence of any tracker_mechanical_damage work orders at Sundowner Mesa in a clean pre-event window.
Comparison of same-storm damage counts per GW at neighbouring sites: Sundowner Mesa materially worse than peers under equal exposure points to H2.

Check whether other fleet sites log zone-level tracker tickets at all; if only Sundowner Mesa does, the denominator/numerator mismatch is confirmed.

hypotheses.statement: A build-lot-specific defect in the KVP-3600 power stage (IGBT module plus its gate driver, plausibly tied to serial prefixes 24xxB/24xxC and firmware rev 4.2.1) causes thermal runaway of the switching devices under summer loading.
predictions: Failing asset serial prefixes (2419B, 2423B, 2428C, 2432C, 2434C) should be over-represented relative to the prefix distribution of all 376 KVP-3600 units in the asset register
Gate driver should be replaced together with the IGBT module in most PART-REPL work orders in this cluster, not the module alone

Repeat failures on the same asset after a module swap should exist (KVP36-2428C-0169 failed 2026-05-23 and again 2026-06-03); more such repeat pairs should appear if the query is run without recurrence-flag filtering
Failures should occur across multiple sites and multiple techs, which they do (5 sites, 7 techs), rather than being confined to one site's install or maintenance crew
Where firmware/rev is recorded, affected units should share rev 4.2.1 and non-affected KVP-3600 units should show a different distribution of revs
discriminating_evidence: Serial-prefix concentration test: if the 8 failures are spread evenly over all prefixes present in the fleet, H1 weakens and H2/H4 strengthen
Presence of thermal-damage work orders on KVP-3600 units in cool-weather months (Nov-Mar) would separate a latent defect from a pure heat-wave driver
Same-site, same-week thermal or derate work orders on non-KVP models would point to H2 rather than a model-specific defect

hypotheses.statement: A discrete late-May-to-June 2026 heat episode across the southern sites drove inverter skid temperatures beyond cooling capacity, and the thermal damage is an environmental over-temperature event rather than a design or lot defect.
predictions: All 8 members fall in a narrow window (2026-05-11 to 2026-06-30) with no KVP-3600 thermal_damage work orders outside it
Other symptoms at the same sites in the same window should spike: high-temp derate, cooling fan failure, HVAC/skid cooling work orders (one member already consumed a cooling fan)
Non-KVP inverter models at Pecan Fork, Joshua Fork, Tidemarsh Bay and Vireo Valley should show elevated thermal/derate/trip work orders in the same weeks, even if coded under a different symptom
Narratives mentioning high_ambient_heat or explicit temperatures (e.g. '104 out there') should cluster on the same calendar days across different sites
discriminating_evidence: Cross-model check at the affected sites: if only KVP-3600 units failed thermally during the heat window while co-located peer models did not, H2 loses to H1
A recurrence of the same cluster in the following summer with no intervening design change would support H2; disappearance after a module/firmware campaign would support H1
Site-level cooling-system PM history: if the affected skids had overdue or skipped HVAC/filter PMs, this becomes a maintenance-driven variant rather than pure weather

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is largely a text- and extraction-artifact: near-identical boilerplate narratives and a keyword-driven symptom mapper assign 'component_thermal_damage' preferentially to KVP-3600 wording, while the same physical failure on peer models is coded under other symptom labels, producing an artificial peer_median_rate of 0.0.
predictions: Several narratives are byte-level near-duplicates ('shut down hard and would not restart. Thermal damage on the power stage. Isolated and locked out pending parts.' appears at least 3 times, and the 'hard faulted / IGBT module N / busbar heat marked / replaced the module and the gate driver' template at least 3 times) — indicating copy-paste or template entry

Follow-up visits to the same asset are counted as independent members (KVP36-2428C-0169 appears twice, KVP36-2419B-0365 twice), so the true distinct-asset count is 6, not 8, dropping the rate to ~0.016

Field-level inconsistencies should be widespread: WO-2026-00514 has resolution_code CLEANED with a gate driver consumed and outcome 'pending'; WO-2026-00522 lists 'DC contactor x4' against an IGBT narrative; WO-2026-00575 is PART-REPL with an empty parts field
A free-text search for 'thermal', 'heat marked', 'cooked', 'discoloured' across peer-model work orders should return hits that were NOT labelled component_thermal_damage
discriminating_evidence: Run the raw-text search on peer models: if peer thermal wording exists but carries other symptom codes, the 0.0 peer median is an artifact and the lift is illusory
De-duplicate by asset and by follow-up chain (isolate/lock-out event plus later parts-fitting visit merged into one failure): if n drops to 5-6 the signal is materially weaker
Check whether the same tech IDs generate the duplicated boilerplate; single-tech authorship of the template points to reporting habit rather than a physical pattern

hypotheses.statement: Eight power-stage failures in 376 units over roughly one quarter is an unremarkable base rate for central inverters, and the apparent lift exists only because peer cohorts are too small for even one expected event, so peer_median_rate is 0.0 by arithmetic rather than by superiority.
predictions: Peer model cohorts should have installed bases well under 376 units; at a pooled rate of ~0.02 per unit per quarter, a 50-unit cohort expects ~1 event and a median of 0 across peers is the most likely outcome
KVP-3600 thermal_damage work orders should appear at a similar per-unit rate in prior periods (2024, 2025) rather than being new in 2026
Fleet-wide, IGBT/gate-driver PART-REPL should be a routine consumable line item with comparable per-unit consumption across models once normalised by unit-years and by inverter rating
The lift field is null, consistent with an undefined ratio against a zero denominator — the ranking is being driven by an uncomputable statistic
discriminating_evidence: Compute exact Poisson tail probability for 8 events in 376 unit-quarters against the fleet pooled rate; a p-value well above 0.05 supports ordinary variation
Compare peer cohort sizes: if any peer model has >300 units and still zero thermal-damage work orders in the same window, the population-size explanation fails and H1 strengthens
Longitudinal rate: a flat KVP-3600 thermal-damage rate across 2024-2026 supports H4; a step change in 2026 supports H1 or H2
Age/operating-hours check: if failing units cluster at high cumulative operating hours near expected IGBT life, this shifts toward end-of-life wear rather than a defect

verdict.reasoning: Every one of the 6 distinct failing assets carries a 24xx serial prefix (2419B-0365, 2423B-0265, 2428C-0169, 2428C-0165, 2432C-0357, 2434C-0084), i.e. 2024-manufacture units, which are only ~179 of the 376 installed KVP-3600s — and the failures are physical, not just textual (IGBT modules and gate drivers consumed in WO-2026-00480, WO-2026-00696, WO-2026-00702, WO-2026-00595). H2 (discrete 2026 heat episode) is weakened because the matched controls show the same thermal family of events on 2024-build units outside the May–June 2026 window and at other sites: WO-2025-00612 (2432C, Jul 2025 overtemp), WO-2025-00847 (2419B, second overtemp of the season, fw 4.2.1), WO-2026-00627 (2422B, second overtemp this season), while the older-build controls (16xx/18xx: WO-2026-00111, WO-2026-00365, WO-2025-00336) show non-thermal or routine findings. H4 (end-of-life wear) fails on direction — the failing population is the newest cohort in the fleet, not the oldest. H3 has real force and is why confidence is only medium: three near-identical boilerplate narratives, follow-up visits double-counted (2428C-0169 in WO-2026-00522 and WO-2026-00575; 2419B-0365 in WO-2026-00480 and WO-2026-00579, so 6 distinct assets not 8), and parts/resolution fields that contradict the text (WO-2026-00522 lists DC contactors against an IGBT narrative; WO-2026-00575 is PART-REPL with no parts; WO-2026-00514 is CLEANED with a gate driver consumed) — but the coding noise does not explain why the thermal-family events land almost exclusively on the 2024 build cohort, and controls WO-2026-00111 and WO-2025-00665 show that identical IGBT failures get coded 'failure_to_start' elsewhere, meaning the true 2024-cohort event count is likely understated rather than inflated.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: The cluster is inflated by follow-up chains and boilerplate: 8 work orders resolve to 6 distinct assets (WO-2026-00522/WO-2026-00575 and WO-2026-00480/WO-2026-00579 are pairs on the same asset), dropping the per-unit rate to ~0.016. Serial prefixes span 2024 weeks 19 through 34 rather than a tight build lot, and 2024 units are ~48% of the fleet, so 6/6 from that cohort is suggestive but not decisive at this n. No peer-model work orders were provided in the control set — every control is another KVP-3600 — so the peer_median_rate of 0.0 and the null lift remain unverified, and the tight May-11-to-Jun-30 window is still fully consistent with H2. Firmware 4.2.1 appears on a control asset too (WO-2025-00847, WO-2024-00195), so firmware alone does not separate members from controls.

population_at_risk.description: KVP-3600 units manufactured in 2024 (24Q1 45 + 24Q2 53 + 24Q3 44 + 24Q4 37), the cohort from which all 6 distinct thermally damaged assets and all three overtemperature-trip control assets are drawn.
population_at_risk.basis: Sum of 2024 manufacture-quarter counts in the supplied installed_base for KVP-3600; failing serial prefixes (2419B, 2423B, 2428C, 2432C, 2434C) all decode to 2024 build weeks present in units_by_2024_manufacture_week.

verdict.recommended_action: Open an OEM engineering review of the power stage and gate-driver thermal design on the 179 2024-build KVP-3600 units, request build records for weeks 19-34 of 2024, and file/preserve warranty claims for the IGBT module and gate-driver replacements in WO-2026-00480, WO-2026-00522, WO-2026-00696 and WO-2026-00702 before next cooling season.
verdict.business_headline: Power-stage thermal failures on KVP-3600 inverters are landing exclusively on the 2024-build cohort (179 of 376 units, ~61 labour hours and multiple IGBT/gate-driver swaps in seven weeks) while older builds show none — worth an OEM engineering review and warranty preservation now, not after next summer.

candidate.label: KVP-3600 manufactured 24Q2 (53 units): hard_fault x5, corrosion_or_wear x5, cooling_airflow_low x5, thermal_derate x4

hypotheses.statement: KVP-3600 units built in 24Q2 carry a build-specific cooling-subsystem defect (fan bearings and/or fan-speed control), which propagates into the thermal symptom chain (low airflow -> derate -> overtemperature trip -> thermal damage / hard fault) at roughly 2.5x the rate of other build quarters.
predictions: Thermal-chain codes (cooling_airflow_low, corrosion_or_wear on cooling_fan, thermal_derate, overtemperature_trip, component_thermal_damage) account for a clearly larger share of 24Q2 work orders than of other-quarter KVP-3600 work orders, while non-thermal codes (ground_fault, grid_ride_through, wildlife_intrusion) sit near peer share.
Fan or fan-bank part replacements on 24Q2 assets occur at a lower asset age (months since commissioning) than the same replacements on 24Q1/24Q3/24Q4 assets.

Repeat/recurrence-flagged work orders concentrate on the same 24Q2 asset IDs (e.g. -0361, -0268 already appear twice in the sample), and derate returns after filter cleaning ('partial_improvement' outcomes) rather than resolving.
Narratives report low airflow with filters described as clean or 'not that dirty' more often in this cohort than in peers — i.e. the airflow loss is not attributable to loading.
OEM escalations / ESCALATED resolution codes for KVP-3600 are disproportionately on 24Q2 serials.
discriminating_evidence: Hold site and calendar month fixed: if 24Q2 units at the same site and season still show elevated thermal work-order rates versus non-24Q2 KVP-3600 units, environment (H2) is excluded.
Normalise by unit-operating-years rather than units: if lift stays near 2.5x, exposure artifacts (H3) are excluded.
Age-align the cohorts: if 24Q2 fan replacements happen at ~12-18 months while peers happen at ~30+ months, expected wear (H4) is excluded.

hypotheses.statement: The 24Q2 cohort was disproportionately deployed to hot, dusty, high-ambient sites (Ashvale Dry Lake, Bitter Draw, Sandhill Bend, Pecan Fork), so the excess is a siting/environment effect during a hot season rather than anything about the build quarter.
predictions: The site distribution of 24Q2 serials differs materially from the site distribution of other KVP-3600 build quarters (a chi-square or simple share comparison shows concentration at the hot-site subset).
Non-24Q2 KVP-3600 units located at the same hot sites show a per-unit work-order rate close to 0.755, not close to the 0.294 peer median.
Thermal-chain work orders in the cohort cluster in Jun-Sep dates, with high_ambient_heat or dust/soiling environment tags over-represented; winter months show near-peer rates.
Other inverter models co-located at those same sites show a parallel summer thermal bulge in the same months.
discriminating_evidence: Site-stratified rate comparison: equal rates for 24Q2 and non-24Q2 units within the same site kills H1; divergence within site kills H2.
Month-of-year profile: if the cohort's excess is flat across all months including winter, a heat/season driver is excluded.
If the excess persists after dropping all work orders tagged high_ambient_heat, H2 is weakened.

hypotheses.statement: The apparent 2.57x lift is an exposure and counting artifact: 24Q2 units have more in-service months and/or a handful of repeat-offender assets and re-opened tickets inflate a 40-work-order count over only 53 units, and the rate per unit-operating-year is unremarkable against peers.
predictions: Mean commissioning-to-present duration for 24Q2 serials exceeds the peer-quarter mean; recomputing rate per unit-year shrinks lift toward ~1.

A small number of asset IDs contribute a disproportionate share of the 40 work orders (sample already shows -0361 and -0268 twice); the count of distinct affected assets is well below 53 and the distinct-asset rate is near peer median.

Some work orders are duplicates/re-opens of the same event (same asset, dates within days, similar narrative and resolution code), or carry NO-FAULT-FOUND / mismatched resolution codes indicating loose ticketing rather than real failures.

The 13 distinct symptoms with no single mode above 5 events is consistent with a generic grab-bag rather than one failure mechanism; no symptom is individually significant against peer symptom shares.
discriminating_evidence: Per-unit-operating-year normalisation and distinct-asset (rather than work-order) counting: if lift survives both, H3 is excluded.
Deduplicate on (asset_id, symptom, 14-day window) and recount; a large drop supports H3.

Check resolution-code/extraction consistency (e.g. WO-2025-00782 coded CLEANED but action part_replaced; WO-2025-01045 coded NO-FAULT-FOUND but a connector was replaced) — high mismatch rates across the corpus indicate the extraction layer, not the fleet, is generating structure.

hypotheses.statement: Cooling fans, bearings and filters are consumables with a roughly 2-year replacement life, and the 24Q2 cohort simply entered its first replacement window inside the observation period, so the cluster is scheduled wear surfacing as corrective work orders.
predictions: Plotting fan-related work orders against asset age (not calendar date) shows the same peak age for 24Q2 and for other build quarters, merely offset in calendar time.
Older build quarters (23Q3/23Q4) show an equal or higher cumulative fan-replacement count per unit once their full age window is included; younger quarters have not yet reached the window.
Fan-replacement work orders resolve cleanly (outcome=resolved, no recurrence flag) and the same asset does not re-fail on the same component within 12 months.
Parts consumption of fans/filters per unit is comparable across build quarters when normalised by unit-operating-years.
discriminating_evidence: Age-aligned hazard curve by build quarter: overlapping curves support H4; an earlier/steeper 24Q2 curve supports H1.
Post-repair recurrence rate: if 24Q2 assets re-derate or re-fail after fan/filter service at a higher rate than peers, ordinary wear is excluded.
Presence of thermal_derate and cooling_airflow_low with clean filters and healthy fans (no consumable at end of life) points away from H4 and toward a control/design defect.

verdict.reasoning: The controls look like the members. The single most damaging comparison is WO-2026-00571 (KVP36-2420B-0352, week 20, in-cohort) against control WO-2026-00586 (KVP36-2427C-0381, week 27, one week outside the Q2 boundary): near-identical afternoon thermal derate, OEM case opened, filters/intakes clear, all fans turning — the control narrative is actually the more detailed of the two, and control WO-2025-00651 (KVP36-2435C-0234) shows the same overtemperature-with-clean-intake pattern on a 24Q3-build unit. The same holds for every non-thermal code in the mix: bird nest in the intake plenum (member WO-2026-00107 vs control WO-2026-00405), ground fault walked/meggered/reset (member WO-2025-01147 vs control WO-2026-00670), AC overcurrent reset with no log pattern (members WO-2024-00196, WO-2026-00286 vs control WO-2025-01166), and grid ride-through self-resync (member WO-2024-00167 vs control WO-2025-00689). H1 requires the thermal chain to be quarter-specific; it is not, and the fan-bearing and airflow events inside the cohort span manufacture weeks 18 through 26 with no lot concentration. H3 also survives on counting: the 22 members shown cover only 18 distinct assets (0265 three times, 0178/0371/0365/0175 twice each), so a 40-work-order count over 53 units is inflated by repeat tickets on a minority of assets, and 13 distinct symptoms with no mode above 5 is a grab-bag, not a failure mechanism. H2 is not needed because the cohort's excess is spread across Vireo Valley, Almond Row and Pine Hollow as well as the hot sites, and H4 cannot be tested without age-aligned curves.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: A residual thermal sub-signal does exist and is not fully explained by artifact: three separate assets logged a repeat 'second overtemp this season, intake and heat sinks clear' (WO-2025-00248, WO-2025-00847, WO-2026-00627), two logged low stack airflow with filters 'not that dirty' after cleaning and only partial improvement (WO-2025-00700, WO-2025-00808), and one asset escalated from thermal damage to a hard shutdown requiring IGBT and power-stage work (WO-2026-00480 then WO-2026-00579). The tech hypothesis of late fan-speed ramp in WO-2025-00248 is plausible. But that pattern appears on 24Q3-build and other-model units in the control set too, so it is a model/fleet question, not a 24Q2 build-quarter question. Peer median of 0.294 is also drawn across 12 quarters, many with 1-5 units, which makes it a noisy baseline; the correct comparison against 24Q1 (45 units), 24Q3 (44) and 24Q4 (37) was not supplied.

population_at_risk.description: No build-quarter-specific at-risk population is established. The thermal phenomenology attributed to 24Q2 is present on non-24Q2 KVP-3600 serials (week 27 and week 35 builds) and on CES40/MGX33 assets in the control set.
population_at_risk.basis: not quantifiable from this data

verdict.recommended_action: Do not open a 24Q2 warranty action; instead re-cut the thermal chain (cooling_airflow_low, thermal_derate, overtemperature_trip, component_thermal_damage) across all KVP-3600 build quarters on a per-unit-operating-year and distinct-asset basis, and only reopen if the late-fan-ramp signal survives that normalisation.
verdict.business_headline: The KVP-3600 24Q2 'defect cohort' does not survive comparison with matched controls — non-24Q2 units one build week apart show the same thermal derate, fan and ground-fault narratives, and the 2.57x lift is driven by repeat tickets on ~18 distinct assets rather than a build-specific failure.

A single property-claim reference (NRS-PL-2025-0417) appears on the earliest, highest-labor tickets and the damage-only inspection walkdowns.

Failure modes are heterogeneous mechanical overload signatures (bent dampers, bent purlins, bent torque tubes, pulled-through clamps, bent limit-switch brackets) rather than one repeated part failing.
discriminating_evidence: Whether any tracker_structure mechanical-damage ticket at this site opens after ~June 2025 without a high_wind or storm environment tag - if the tail truly ends, H1 survives and H2 weakens.
Whether the same asset_ids re-appear in later wind events at lower recorded wind speeds (supports H2 over H1).
Whether prior-year records show a comparable burst at this site after any prior wind event (recurring event response = H1; first-ever = ambiguous).

hypotheses.statement: The trackers at Sundowner Mesa have a design or installation weakness - rows failing to reach full stow, plus undersized dampers and limit-switch brackets - so a sub-design-wind event produced damage that a compliant tracker population would not have sustained, and the same modes will recur at lower wind speeds.
predictions: Narratives explicitly recording incomplete stow ('rows caught partway to stow') appear on more than a handful of tickets, and stow-related symptoms recur in subsequent, milder wind days.

The 'limit switch bracket bent / reformed / recalibrated' mode recurs on tracker rows already repaired during the burst (repeat asset_id within 6-12 months, recurrence flag true) - one member already carries recurrence=true.
Part consumption is dominated by a narrow set of SKUs (damper, coupling, limit-switch bracket, stow pin) rather than broad structural steel, indicating a repeating weak link.
Sister sites sharing the same tracker OEM/vintage show elevated tracker_structure ticket rates per installed row even in months with no logged wind event.
Post-burst preventive-maintenance or retrofit work orders (stow-logic change, damper upgrade) appear in the record within 6 months.
discriminating_evidence: Normalised ticket rate per installed tracker row at this site versus other sites of the same OEM/vintage in wind-free months: elevated => H2; equal => H1 or H3.
Repeat-visit rate on the same asset_id after the burst closes - high repeat rate is the strongest separator from a one-off event.
Whether recorded/estimated wind speed on 3/14 exceeded the tracker's rated stow wind speed; damage below rating supports H2.

hypotheses.statement: The burst count is largely an administrative artifact: insurance-claim documentation (NRS-PL-2025-0417) forced one work order per row/zone at a finer granularity than the site's normal batching, so ticket count spiked while actual damaged-asset count and true labor were far smaller than 27 discrete faults imply.
predictions: Mean labor per ticket in the burst (111.6 h / 27 = 4.1 h) is comparable to or lower than the site's normal tracker_structure ticket, and several tickets carry 1.6-2.6 h - i.e. no evidence of unusually heavy per-ticket work.

Multiple work orders in the window reference the same claim number, and some reference zone-level assets (TR-Z02, TR-Z08, TR-Z09) that each already cover 'six rows' or 'nine rows' - so row-level and zone-level tickets double-count the same physical damage.

Internal field inconsistency consistent with hasty claim-driven entry: parts_used populated while resolution_code is ADJUSTED, resolution_code NO-FAULT-FOUND on a ticket whose narrative describes a replaced stow pin, an Inspection-type ticket coded SW-UPDATE with a coupling consumed.
Ticket-per-day counts spike on days when a claims adjuster or walkdown activity is logged, not on days following weather.
lost_mwh_reported_total (69.7 MWh over 27 tickets) is allocated in round or repeated per-ticket amounts rather than derived from distinct outage durations.
discriminating_evidence: De-duplicate by physical asset (expand zone-level tickets into their constituent rows and remove overlaps): if the distinct-damaged-row count is far below or far above 27, the raw ticket count is not a reliable severity signal.
Compare ticket granularity for tracker_structure before vs during the window at the same site - a shift from zone-batched to row-level tickets confirms H3.
Presence/absence of the claim reference on tickets is correlated with ticket granularity.

hypotheses.statement: A single technician (TECH-0231 authored the majority of sampled tickets) used copy-paste narrative templates and retro-attributed routine, pre-existing tracker misalignment and stall work to the March wind event, so an unknown fraction of the 27 tickets is ordinary maintenance re-labelled as storm damage.
predictions: Near-verbatim narrative strings repeat across multiple tickets ('not tracking, limit switch bracket bent. Reformed the bracket and recalibrated the row', 'torque tube out of true at the third bearing. Shimmed and realigned') on different asset_ids and different dates.
Ticket authorship is heavily concentrated: one tech accounts for a disproportionate share of the 27 relative to that tech's share of all site work orders in the same period.

Later tickets in the window carry environment='none_mentioned' yet narrative framing like 'Same as the others this month' or 'Post event walkdown' that asserts event linkage without independent damage evidence.
The same repeated failure modes appear in that tech's tickets at this site before 2025-03-15 and after the window closes, at a low but non-zero rate.
Symptom mix drifts over the window from tracker_mechanical_damage (early, wind-tagged) toward tracker_misalignment / tracker_stall (late, untagged).
discriminating_evidence: Split the 27 by author and by narrative-template fingerprint: if removing one tech's templated tickets collapses the burst below the detection threshold, the cluster is partly a reporting effect rather than a physical one.
Cross-check late-window tickets against SCADA/tracker-controller fault timestamps - faults first appearing before 2025-03-14 indicate retro-attribution.
Whether independent evidence (photos, claim line items, parts issued from stores) exists for the untagged late tickets as it does for the early wind-tagged ones.

verdict.reasoning: The burst is explicitly and repeatedly self-described as remediation of a single convective wind event: WO-2025-00214, WO-2025-00218 and WO-2025-00240 name the March 14 microburst, a met-station peak near 71 mph, and a single property-claim reference (NRS-PL-2025-0417), and the damage modes are heterogeneous mechanical-overload signatures (bent dampers WO-2025-00257/WO-2025-00269, bent purlins WO-2025-00223/WO-2025-00268, pulled-through clamps WO-2025-00289/WO-2025-00368, damaged stow pins WO-2025-00284/WO-2025-00285) rather than one part failing repeatedly, which is what H2 would require. Arrival decays from a mid-March peak to scattered late-April cleanup (WO-2025-00368, WO-2025-00375, WO-2025-00383), consistent with a fixed damage population being worked down. H3 and H4 are partially correct and further deflate the headline count: zone-level tickets (WO-2025-00218 TR-Z08, WO-2025-00258 TR-Z09, WO-2025-00293 TR-Z02, WO-2025-00383 TR-Z07) each cover six-to-nine rows and overlap row-level tickets, TECH-0231 authored nearly all members with near-verbatim narratives (WO-2025-00286, WO-2025-00302, WO-2025-00339, WO-2025-00344, WO-2025-00375 are the same limit-switch sentence), so 27 tickets is not 27 distinct faults. The controls are largely uninformative for component match, but the one directly comparable control — WO-2025-00447, a post-storm walkdown at Hollowell Ranch that found zero structural damage — shows post-event walkdowns at other sites do not generate damage tickets absent a severe local event, which supports an event-specific rather than fleet-wide cause.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Two members (WO-2025-00218, WO-2025-00240) record 'rows caught partway to stow' at a peak of roughly 71 mph, which is below the stow rating of most utility trackers and is the one genuine H2-flavoured signal in the set; if rows did not reach stow, damage severity may reflect a stow-logic or actuation weakness rather than pure wind loading. The late-window limit-switch-bracket mode (WO-2025-00286, WO-2025-00302, WO-2025-00339, WO-2025-00344, WO-2025-00375) carries environment='none_mentioned' and could be an emerging mode rather than storm tail. Data hygiene is poor enough to weaken any reading: WO-2025-00285 is coded NO-FAULT-FOUND on a narrative describing a replaced stow pin, WO-2025-00214 lists 'tracker motor x3' against a claim-documentation narrative, and WO-2025-00324 lists a bearing housing against a shim-and-realign narrative.

population_at_risk.description: No ongoing at-risk population identified; the damaged asset population is closed and already bounded by property claim NRS-PL-2025-0417.
population_at_risk.basis: not quantifiable from this data - zone-level tickets (TR-Z02, TR-Z07, TR-Z08, TR-Z09) overlap row-level tickets, so distinct damaged rows cannot be counted without de-duplication, and no installed_base was supplied.

verdict.recommended_action: Close the burst as storm remediation under claim NRS-PL-2025-0417, and monitor Sundowner Mesa tracker_structure tickets for the next two quarters for wind-independent limit-switch-bracket or incomplete-stow reports, re-opening as an engineering assessment only if that mode recurs.
verdict.business_headline: The 27-ticket March tracker spike at Sundowner Mesa is cleanup from one microburst already under an open property claim, not an emerging tracker defect, and the count is inflated by zone-level and templated duplicate tickets.

candidate.label: TECH-0231 logs tracker work per ROW (91%) vs fleet 51%

hypotheses.statement: The 51% fleet baseline is not a comparable denominator: TECH-0231's queue is almost purely tracker work (where a row asset ID exists), while the fleet figure pools work types/assets for which row-level tagging is impossible or meaningless, so the 91% vs 51% gap is a work-mix artifact rather than a behavioural difference.

Other technicians whose WOs are filtered to tracker-only work should also show row-share well above 0.51.

If TECH-0231 still sits far above peers after work-type stratification, H1 is falsified.

hypotheses.statement: The 'granularity' field is derived from narrative text parsing, and TECH-0231 simply has the habit of opening every narrative with the row tag ("TR-B0x-Rxxx ..."), so the metric measures writing style rather than actual CMMS asset assignment.
predictions: In TECH-0231's records the asset_id field should be reproducible from the first token of the narrative in a very high fraction of rows (13/14 in the sample begin with the row tag).
Technicians with low row-share should show narratives that mention rows in free text but carry block- or site-level asset_id values, i.e. narrative and asset_id disagree more often.
Other TECH-0231 metadata should show similar template regularity (repeated stock phrases such as 'verified through a full sweep', which appears in ~6/14 sampled narratives).

Extraction noise should be visible independently: sampled rows already contain resolution_code/action contradictions (NO-FAULT-FOUND with 'part_replaced', 'tracker motor x3' as parts on a damper job), indicating the structured fields are partly machine-inferred.
discriminating_evidence: Check whether asset_id was entered at WO creation (dispatch timestamp) or populated later/derived; if asset_id predates the narrative, style cannot be the cause and H2 fails.
Compare field-level provenance: if low-row-share techs' narratives contain row tags at the same rate as TECH-0231's, the difference is parsing/entry, not observation.

hypotheses.statement: A discrete high-wind event on 2025-03-14 at Sundowner Mesa generated an insurance claim (NRS-PL-2025-0417) that required per-row damage documentation, and TECH-0231 was the assigned claim technician, so the row-level logging is a time-bounded claim-handling artifact concentrated in the Mar-Jun 2025 window.
predictions: TECH-0231's row-share should be strongly time-varying: near 1.0 for WOs dated 2025-03-15 through roughly 2025-06, and closer to the fleet baseline for 2026 WOs.
A disproportionate share of the 41 members should cluster at Sundowner Mesa in a ~10-week block after 2025-03-14, with tracker_mechanical_damage symptoms.
Other technicians working the same event window at Sundowner Mesa should also show elevated row-share, and their row-share should drop afterward too.
Claim references or 'event/cleanup' language should co-occur with the earliest members (present in WO-2025-00214 and WO-2025-00368).
discriminating_evidence: Split TECH-0231's 41 WOs into pre/post 2025-07 cohorts: if 2026 WOs (e.g. Ashvale Dry Lake, Joshua Fork) still run ~90% row-level, the event cannot be the driver and H3 loses to H1/H2/H4.
Check whether row-share elevation is shared with other techs in the same event window (event-driven) or unique to TECH-0231 (personal habit).

hypotheses.statement: The effect is a site/assignment confound: the three sites TECH-0231 works (Sundowner Mesa, Joshua Fork, Ashvale Dry Lake) have their tracker assets registered down to the row in the CMMS hierarchy, while other fleet sites are registered at block level, so any technician assigned there would show ~90% row-level logging.
predictions: Row-share computed per site should be near 0.9 at Sundowner Mesa, Joshua Fork and Ashvale Dry Lake and well below 0.51 at the remaining fleet sites.
Other technicians with WOs at these three sites should show row-share statistically indistinguishable from TECH-0231's 0.91.
The asset register for these sites should contain distinct TR-Bxx-Rxxx entries; low-row-share sites should have no such per-row asset records to select.
If TECH-0231 has any WOs at a block-level site, those specific WOs should be logged at block granularity.
discriminating_evidence: Fit row-share by site and by technician jointly: if the site term absorbs the effect and the technician term shrinks to noise, H4 wins over H2.
Look for a technician at these sites with low row-share; a single such counterexample argues the registry permits both granularities and pushes the explanation back to individual habit (H2).

verdict.reasoning: The controls show that granularity tracks the scope of the job, not the technician: at the very same sites, other techs log single-row jobs at row level (WO-2024-00118 TR-B03-R090 by TECH-0103, WO-2024-00125 TR-B02-R078 by TECH-0194, WO-2025-00505 TR-B04-R096 by TECH-0187) while zone- or block-scope work is logged at zone/block level (WO-2025-00294 TR-Z04, WO-2025-00383 TR-Z07 'nine rows needed attention', WO-2024-00280 TR-Z01, WO-2025-00219 TR-Z05, WO-2024-00334 blank/B05). TECH-0231's own control confirms this: when the scope was a block-wide torque audit he logged at block level (WO-2026-00623, asset 'B04'), which is what H2's pure-writing-style story would not predict. His 41 members are almost entirely single-row tracker CM/PM tasks (WO-2025-00223, WO-2025-00272, WO-2026-00334, WO-2026-00617), so the 91% simply reflects a queue of row-scoped tracker work compared against a fleet denominator that pools zone walkdowns and non-row-taggable assets. H3 is falsified because row-level logging persists across 2026 at Ashvale Dry Lake and Joshua Fork (WO-2026-00052, WO-2026-00171, WO-2026-00617), far outside the March 2025 wind-event window; H4 is falsified because both granularities coexist at Sundowner Mesa and Ashvale Dry Lake in the controls.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Several member records show internally inconsistent structured fields - WO-2025-00285 carries resolution_code NO-FAULT-FOUND with action 'part_replaced', and WO-2025-00214 lists 'tracker motor x3' on a structural/claim documentation job with resolution ADJUSTED - indicating some structured fields are machine-inferred rather than entered. That is a genuine extraction-quality concern (partial support for H2), but it is present in controls too (e.g. WO-2024-00125 NO-FAULT-FOUND with 'drive replaced', WO-2024-00280 PART-REPL on a grease PM) and is therefore fleet-wide noise, not a TECH-0231 behaviour.

population_at_risk.description: No physical asset population is at risk; this candidate concerns a logging-metric denominator, not equipment condition.
population_at_risk.basis: not quantifiable from this data

verdict.recommended_action: Retire or re-stratify the technician row-share KPI so it is computed only within single-row-scope tracker work orders, rather than against a mixed fleet denominator that includes zone- and block-scope jobs.
verdict.business_headline: TECH-0231's 91% row-level logging is a work-mix artifact - peers at the same sites log row-level on row-scoped jobs and zone-level on zone-scoped jobs - so no technician coaching or commercial action is warranted; fix the metric instead.

candidate.label: KVP-3600 manufactured 24Q3 (44 units): hard_fault x5, component_thermal_damage x5, ground_fault x3, overtemperature_trip x3

hypotheses.statement: KVP-3600 units built in 24Q3 carry a thermal-management defect (undersized/mis-controlled cooling path or fan-control firmware rev 4.2.1) that drives a repeatable chain of low airflow -> thermal derate -> IGBT/busbar thermal damage -> hard fault, and the same defect pits DC contactors.
predictions: The thermal-family symptoms (cooling_airflow_low, thermal_derate, overtemperature_trip, component_thermal_damage, hard_fault) together account for the large majority of the cohort's excess over peer_median_rate, while non-thermal symptoms (ground_fault, wildlife, undervoltage) are at or below peer rates.
Narratives repeatedly record clean filters/clear plenum/all fans turning alongside high cabinet temperature, i.e. cooling faults with no found obstruction, at a higher share than in peer cohorts.
Damage localises to the same physical position across assets (e.g. 'IGBT module 2', busbar heat marking) in multiple distinct asset_ids, not just repeat visits to one unit.
Assets whose narratives mention a firmware rev other than 4.2.1 (or a post-update WO) show a lower subsequent thermal WO rate than assets still on 4.2.1.
Time-from-commissioning to first thermal WO is similar across cohort assets (a wear-out/defect clock), rather than randomly scattered.
Escalations, Warranty-type WOs and OEM case references appear preferentially on the thermal subset.
discriminating_evidence: Thermal WO rate for 24Q3 units remains ~2x peer after restricting to sites that also host non-24Q3 KVP-3600 units (same-site, same-model comparison).
Peer-quarter KVP-3600 units at the SAME hot sites (Bitter Draw, Joshua Fork) do NOT show derate/IGBT damage — kills the siting explanation.
Counting distinct asset_ids rather than WOs still leaves >2x the peer per-unit rate — kills the repeat-visit inflation explanation.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is largely a counting and extraction artifact: 30 work orders spread over few distinct assets (repeat visits, warranty follow-ups, escalate-then-return pairs) plus mis-extracted symptom/parts fields inflate an apparent 0.682/unit rate that, per distinct affected asset and after de-duplication, is near the peer median.
predictions: Distinct asset_ids in the cohort are materially fewer than 30 (e.g. KVP36-2428C-0169 appears twice within 11 days, KVP36-2432C-0357 and KVP36-2434C-0084 each appear twice), so WOs-per-affected-asset exceeds the peer figure while affected-assets/44 does not.
Multi-WO chains share a single failure event: an ESCALATED/pending outcome followed within days-weeks by a PART-REPL on the same asset_id, same component.

parts_used and narrative disagree in a measurable fraction of cohort records (WO-2026-00522 parts 'DC contactor x4' vs IGBT narrative; WO-2026-00690 parts 'gate driver' vs contactor narrative), indicating the structured symptom/component fields are unreliable for this cohort.

The 13 distinct symptoms include single-count entries (wildlife_intrusion, no_fault_found, overcurrent_trip, undervoltage_trip) that are grab-bag filler; removing single-count symptoms drops n substantially and lift below ~1.5.
Cohort membership is defined by asset_id prefix parsing; some KVP36-24xx serials may be misassigned to 24Q3 versus adjacent quarters.
discriminating_evidence: Collapse WOs to unique failure events (same asset, same component, within 30 days) and recompute rate: if it lands near 0.29-0.35, the cluster is bookkeeping, not hardware.
Check whether peer quarters were counted with the same de-duplication rule; asymmetric counting would explain lift on its own.
Re-derive mfg_quarter from a commissioning/nameplate field independent of the serial string and see whether the 44-unit cohort membership survives.

hypotheses.statement: The 24Q3 build was shipped disproportionately to hot, high-irradiance or dusty sites, so the excess is an ambient-environment and duty-cycle effect on ordinary hardware rather than a build-quarter defect.
predictions: Cohort assets concentrate at a small number of sites (Tidemarsh Bay, Joshua Fork, Bitter Draw, Sandhill Bend appear repeatedly across only 14 sampled WOs).
Thermal-family WO dates cluster in the warm months (the sample's thermal WOs fall May-Sep 2025/2026; ground-fault and reset WOs spread more evenly).
Narratives for thermal events mention high_ambient_heat, afternoon timing, or self-recovery after sundown at above-baseline frequency.
Non-KVP models at the same sites show elevated thermal_derate/overtemperature rates in the same months.
Site-stratified rate for the cohort converges toward peer_median_rate once each site's own baseline thermal rate is subtracted.
discriminating_evidence: Compare 24Q3 units against other-quarter KVP-3600 units co-located at the same sites; equal rates support H3, higher 24Q3 rates support H1.
If cohort units at cool/coastal sites (Tidemarsh Bay) show the same IGBT thermal damage as desert sites, ambient is not the driver.
A summer-only excess with no winter excess favours H3; a year-round excess favours H1.

hypotheses.statement: This is ordinary variation plus a site-level installation-workmanship issue: with only 44 units the observed count is within plausible Poisson/overdispersion range of the peer median, and the ground-fault subset traces to pinched DC connectors in combiner boxes (an installer defect shared with non-cohort equipment), not to the inverter build quarter.
predictions: Recomputing per-unit rates for all 12 peer quarters shows several quarters near or above 0.68, i.e. the cohort sits inside the spread of quarter-to-quarter rates rather than being an outlier against a tight distribution.
Ground-fault WOs resolve to combiner-box connector damage (CB-B05-12, CB-B06-15) or to NO-FAULT-FOUND resets, with no inverter component implicated.
The same pinched-connector/combiner ground-fault signature appears on other models and other build quarters at Pine Hollow, Chestnut Hollow and Sandhill Bend during the same period.

A large share of cohort WOs close as RESET or NO-FAULT-FOUND with low labor hours, consistent with nuisance events rather than hardware failure (mean labor here is ~6.3 h across 30 WOs, ~188 h total, modest for 30 hardware failures).
Lost MWh per WO (~2.5) is comparable to peer-quarter WOs of the same symptom types.
discriminating_evidence: An exact Poisson/negative-binomial test of 30 events on 44 units against the peer-quarter rate distribution: a p-value that is unremarkable after multiple-comparison correction across all model/quarter cells argues the cluster was found by searching, not by a real defect.
If ground faults are excluded and the residual thermal excess is still significant, H4 fails for the thermal subset while remaining valid for the ground-fault subset.
Whether combiner-box connector faults at those sites are model-agnostic (supports H4) or occur only under KVP 24Q3 skids (supports H1).

verdict.reasoning: The cohort's excess is not a grab-bag: roughly two-thirds of the shown members sit on one causal chain — low airflow with clean filters/clear plenum/all six fans turning (WO-2025-00862, WO-2025-00920), afternoon derate (WO-2025-00670, WO-2025-00908), then power-stage thermal damage and hard faults (WO-2026-00514, WO-2026-00522, WO-2026-00575, WO-2026-00696, WO-2026-00626, WO-2026-00677), plus a DC contactor with pitted contacts described as 'running hot a while' (WO-2026-00690). Two distinct assets at two distinct sites show the same localised damage — 'IGBT module 2 ... busbar heat marked' (WO-2026-00522 at Joshua Fork, WO-2026-00696 at Vireo Valley) — which is hard to explain by repeat-visit inflation (H2) and points at a common build/design feature. H3 is weakened because the same power-stage thermal damage appears at cool coastal Tidemarsh Bay (WO-2026-00514, WO-2026-00626) and at Frostline Prairie (WO-2025-00833), not only at desert sites. H2 and H4 are partly right and I have discounted the cluster accordingly: the ground-fault members are model- and quarter-agnostic combiner/string issues indistinguishable from controls (members WO-2025-00158, WO-2025-00460 vs controls WO-2026-00462, WO-2025-00378), and repeat visits are real (KVP36-2428C-0169 in WO-2025-00908/WO-2026-00522/WO-2026-00575; KVP36-2432C-0357 in WO-2025-00612/WO-2026-00514/WO-2026-00626) — but even collapsing to distinct assets the shown 22 WOs map to 15 assets, and the 11-day repeat hard failure on 0169 after an IGBT/gate-driver replacement is recurrence, not double-counting. Escalation is warranted mainly because the failing units are still inside OEM parts warranty (WO-2026-00626, WO-2026-00677 both opened Kelvara cases with authorised swaps), so the commercial window is open now.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: The 'fan bank running, filters not that dirty, temps came down some' narrative is reproduced almost verbatim on a non-cohort unit in the controls (WO-2025-00700, KVP36-2419B-0373, a 2024 week-19 build), so that symptom is not unique to 24Q3 and may be a boilerplate narrative pattern. Ground faults in the cluster (WO-2025-00158 pinched connector in CB-B05-12, WO-2025-00460 nothing found) match controls exactly (WO-2026-00462 chafed home run CB-B03-17, WO-2025-00378 megger ok reset held) and should be stripped from the cohort signal. Repeat visits are heavy — at least 5 assets account for 12 of the 22 shown WOs — so the 0.682 WO-per-unit rate overstates the affected-asset rate. Peer per-quarter rates for the comparably large 24Q1 (45 units), 24Q2 (53) and 24Q4 (37) cohorts were not shown individually, so the 2.32x lift against a 12-quarter median is not yet a clean like-for-like test.

verdict.recommended_action: Open a cohort-level warranty case with Kelvara covering all 44 KVP-3600 24Q3 units citing the repeated 'IGBT module 2 / busbar heat marked' signature and fan-control rev 4.2.1, and inspect the remaining ~29 un-ticketed cohort units for heat-marked busbars, pitted DC contactors and firmware revision.
verdict.business_headline: A 44-unit KVP-3600 24Q3 build is failing power stages from a repeatable cooling-then-IGBT-damage chain across both hot and coastal sites while still under parts warranty — file the cohort claim before the window closes.

hypotheses.statement: A defective or under-specified grease/seal package on one lot of tracker slew drives — concentrated in blocks B04 and B06 at Ashvale Dry Lake — is drying out and hardening early, producing genuine drive-drive failures at ~9x fleet rate.
predictions: Affected asset_ids cluster in a subset of blocks (B04/B06 supply 6 of 8 here); a block-level breakdown of the site's full tracker population shows drive WOs disproportionate to trackers installed per block.

Narratives should repeatedly report irreversible damage, not just dry lube: 'gear faces scored', 'backlash out of spec', and parts_used='gearbox'/drive replacement in a substantial fraction (2 of 8 sampled already show this).
Repeat WOs on the same asset_id, or on adjacent row numbers (R090/R095/R096), should appear within 12-24 months with recurrence flags true.
Other Ashvale symptoms on non-drive components (inverter, combiner, module) should NOT be elevated versus fleet — the excess is component-specific.
If commissioning/install dates are available, affected assets share a narrow install window or drive vendor/serial band.

Presence of hard-failure evidence (scored gears, gearbox parts consumed, replacement rather than repack) separates a true defect from a mere lubrication-service backlog (H4).
Recurrence on the same asset after a clean-and-repack indicates the failure mechanism persists; one-and-done fixes argue against a defective drive lot.

hypotheses.statement: Ashvale's dry-lakebed setting drives abrasive alkali dust into drive housings, degrading grease site-wide — an expected site-environment effect rather than an equipment defect, and one that should be managed by a shortened relube interval.
predictions: Affected trackers are spread across most blocks and row numbers rather than clustered in one install lot.

Narratives contain abrasion/contamination language ('gritty', 'dried out', 'contaminated', 'dust') at a higher rate than the same symptom at other sites; at least one sampled WO already says 'dried out and gritty'.
Ashvale should also show elevated rates for other dust-mediated symptoms (module soiling, bearing/bushing wear, seal or actuator contamination) relative to fleet, not just drive grease.
Event dates should skew toward the dry/windy season or follow high-wind periods; the sample spans Jul/Aug/Nov/Apr/Jun/Nov/Jan, so a seasonality test is directly checkable.
Any other site in the corpus with a similar arid descriptor/geography should show a comparable drive_grease_degradation rate.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is largely a labelling/reporting artifact: one technician (TECH-0194, 5 of 8 WOs) writes a fixed template phrase for any noisy drive, so ordinary drive complaints at Ashvale get coded 'drive_grease_degradation' while equivalent events elsewhere land under other symptom labels.

verdict.reasoning: The matched controls kill the site-specificity claim: the exact same failure mode, with near-identical wording, appears at Dry Creek Junction (WO-2024-00073, WO-2025-00535), Tallow Branch (WO-2025-01161) and Red Clay Flats (WO-2025-00728), where techs explicitly call it 'normal wear for the vintage' and 'the fourth one this quarter' — so drive grease hardening is a fleet-wide, cross-site phenomenon, not an Ashvale environmental or lot effect (defeating H1 and H2).
