verdict.reasoning: Five of the eight members are MV collector/switchgear events (WO-2024-00060, WO-2025-00298, WO-2025-00317, WO-2025-00705, WO-2025-00837) spanning blocks B01, B03, B04 and the main feeder, with physical evidence of termination workmanship: an MV termination kit x3 consumed on WO-2025-00317, a failed switchgear termination replaced on WO-2025-00837, and two independent cable faults located at roughly the same run position (~300 ft in from the block end) on different circuits — H1's discriminating signature. Stripping the MV/conductor WOs leaves only three inverter-level faults (WO-2024-00188 string self-stop, WO-2025-00351 OEM warranty control board, WO-2025-00614 gate driver) over 3.5 GW-months, i.e. essentially the fleet baseline of 0.63/GW-month, which is what H4 and H3 would have to explain away and cannot. H2 has real support — WO-2025-00298 and WO-2025-00317 are near-identical four days apart — but the controls show the same boilerplate reuse fleet-wide (WO-2024-00188 at Vireo is textually the same event write-up as control WO-2025-00695 at Sandhill Bend; controls WO-2026-00049 and WO-2025-00882 are the same DC-GF template at two different sites; WO-2026-00030 and WO-2025-00320 are the same PM template), so templating is a corpus-wide style, not a Vireo-specific inflation mechanism, and even collapsing that one pair leaves four MV events on three separate blocks. The control set contains no MV collector or switchgear faults at any comparison site — every non-Vireo control is DC-side, inverter thermal, or PM — which is the strongest argument that the MV concentration is local to Vireo rather than an artifact of how faults are coded.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: WO-2025-00298 and WO-2025-00317 are near-identical narratives four days apart and may be one event double-booked, which would cut the MV count from 5 to 4; WO-2024-00060 and WO-2025-00705 are also near-identical text (a year apart, different techs), so at least part of the cluster's coherence is narrative templating rather than confirmed distinct events. Exposure is only 3.5 GW-months, so the Poisson interval on a lift of 3.65 is wide. Both April 2025 cable faults are still 'pending' with contractors scheduled, so no confirmed root cause has been returned, and the recurring overnight feeder trips (WO-2024-00060, WO-2025-00705) explicitly closed with 'no root cause established' — they could be a grid-side or relay-setting issue rather than a cable defect.

population_at_risk.description: MV collector circuits at Vireo Valley implicated by member narratives: block feeders B01, B03, B04, plus the main feeder / switchgear bus. Inverter installed-base tables (KVP-3600, MG-3300) are not the exposed population here — the residual inverter fault rate at this site is at baseline.
population_at_risk.basis: Count of distinct circuit/block identifiers named in cluster narratives: B01 (WO-2025-00298), B03 (WO-2025-00317), B04 (WO-2025-00837), main feeder (WO-2024-00060, WO-2025-00705). Total MV circuit length and splice count at the site are not quantifiable from this data.

verdict.recommended_action: Commission VLF tan-delta and partial-discharge testing plus a termination/splice audit on the Vireo Valley MV collector circuits serving B01, B03 and B04 and the main feeder, and pull the EPC construction records for those pulls to establish whether the terminations fall under the original installation warranty.
verdict.business_headline: Vireo Valley's 3.6x hard-fault rate is not an inverter problem — five of eight events are MV collector cable and switchgear terminations across three blocks, including two cable faults at the same run position on different circuits, and the site's inverter fault rate is at fleet baseline once those are removed.

hypotheses.statement: Coralito Flats has a genuine physical-layer defect in its serial/daisy-chain comms network (marginal terminations, connector corrosion, or grounding/surge exposure) concentrated in a few blocks, producing repeat self-clearing dropouts on the same assets and zones.
predictions: The 13 WOs should concentrate on a small number of repeated asset_ids / block prefixes (B01, B03, B05, B06) rather than being spread uniformly across the site's asset population.
Assets that appear once should have an elevated probability of appearing again within 90 days; recurrence flags should be true for a majority of members and should cluster by block.
Resolution codes tied to physical intervention (reseated daisy chain, comms module parts, surge card) should be present and should grow as a share of comms_loss WOs over the 2024-2026 window.
Other symptoms on the same assets (tracker misalignment, inverter derate) should be rare or absent, i.e. the assets themselves are healthy while only the comms path fails.
Comms-module and surge-card parts consumption at this site should exceed the fleet per-GW-month rate.
discriminating_evidence: Asset-level repeat count: high concentration (few assets, many hits) supports H1; 13 distinct assets spread across the site undercuts it.
Presence of hardware parts issued or physical repairs (reseat, replace) versus pure RESET/NO-FAULT-FOUND closures.
Whether comms_loss WOs at this site trend upward over time (degrading physical layer) or stay flat.

hypotheses.statement: These are nuisance telemetry dropouts with no equipment fault: the assets keep producing while flagged offline, and the site's SCADA alarm/dispatch configuration converts self-clearing comms gaps into truck-roll work orders that other fleet sites do not raise.
predictions: Reported lost_mwh should be ~0 for nearly every member, with essentially all of the 35.2 MWh attributable to the single 2025-04-24 lightning WO.
Mean labor hours per WO (~2.3) should be at or below the site's overall CM average, and well below the fleet CM average for genuine hardware failures.
Resolution codes should be dominated by RESET / NO-FAULT-FOUND / SW-UPDATE with empty parts_used fields; outcome 'resolved' or 'recurring' with no replacement.
Narratives should repeatedly assert the asset was operating normally while showing offline ('inverting fine', 'come back on their own', 'no production lost').
Priority distribution should skew P3/P4, inconsistent with a fault causing real generation loss.
discriminating_evidence: Any member WO with material reported lost_mwh or a confirmed production stoppage would falsify H2 and favour H1.
Compare lost_mwh per comms_loss WO at Coralito versus fleet comms_loss WOs: if Coralito's is materially lower, the site is logging events other sites ignore.
Presence versus absence of parts issued: sustained zero-parts closures support H2.

hypotheses.statement: The lift is a logging-practice artifact: a small number of technicians at this site (TECH-0110, TECH-0159, TECH-0222) open an individual CM work order for every comms alarm, including duplicate 'same units dropping out again' entries, inflating the counted event rate without a change in underlying equipment behaviour.
predictions: Three or fewer tech IDs should account for the large majority of the 13 members; those same techs should show elevated WO-per-labor-hour counts across all symptoms, not just comms_loss.
Multiple members should be batch/duplicate logs referencing groups of units ('same units in B03/B06/B01') rather than a single discrete asset event, so counted 'events' overstate distinct incidents.
Coralito's total WO count per GW-month across all symptoms should also be above fleet, not just comms_loss; if only comms_loss is elevated, H3 weakens.
The same techs, if they have worked other sites, should show comparable comms_loss logging rates there.
discriminating_evidence: Site-wide WO rate across all symptoms: broadly elevated => H3; comms_loss uniquely elevated => H1 or H2.
Tech mobility check — comms_loss rate follows the technician between sites (H3) or stays with the site regardless of technician (H1/H2).
Count of members that are group/blanket logs versus single-asset incidents.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is ordinary Poisson variation on a small exposure base (13 events over 3.7 GW-months) amplified by one discrete lightning event, and the site's rate is not distinguishable from the fleet rate once that event and its follow-ons are removed.
predictions: A Poisson confidence interval on 13 counts over 3.7 GW-months should be wide enough that its lower bound approaches the fleet rate of 0.95; other sites with comparable small exposure should show similarly extreme lifts in both directions.
Removing the 2025-04-24 lightning WO and any comms WOs on the same assets in the following 60 days should drop the site rate materially toward fleet.
Members should be spread thinly across ~24 months with no sustained monthly acceleration; a naive month-by-month count should look like scattered singletons.
Weather-tagged members should be a small minority (one in this sample), and the remainder should carry environment 'none_mentioned'.
discriminating_evidence: Rank Coralito's lift against the lift distribution of all similarly-sized site/symptom cells: if several small-exposure cells show lift >3, the finding is a population-size effect.
Recompute site rate excluding storm-linked WOs — a large drop favours H4, a small drop favours H1/H2.
Temporal test: a rising or block-concentrated trend contradicts H4 and supports a persistent site-level cause.

verdict.reasoning: The members are almost uniformly self-clearing telemetry dropouts with no production consequence: narratives explicitly state the asset was healthy while flagged offline (WO-2024-00292 'inverting fine the whole time it showed offline', WO-2025-00125, WO-2024-00270 'no production lost', WO-2025-00793 and WO-2025-00849 'they come back on their own'), closures are RESET/NO-FAULT-FOUND/SW-UPDATE with essentially no parts, and labor is ~1-3 hours per visit. H1 (concentrated physical defect) is weakened because the 13 members hit 13 distinct asset IDs spread across B01/B03/B05/B06/B07 and the zone controllers rather than a few repeat offenders, and only two WOs involved any physical intervention (daisy-chain reseats, WO-2025-01128 and WO-2026-00042). H3 is not supported as a pure logging artifact because the controls show the same site-level phenomenon under different symptom labels with different techs (WO-2025-01066 'third comms alarm at this site in two months with no explanation', WO-2024-00178 humid-night mass dropout with no production loss, WO-2025-00116 RTU lockup) - the dropouts are real events, they are just non-productive to dispatch on. H4 is only partially right: removing the one discrete lightning event (WO-2025-00372) leaves 12 routine nuisance calls, so the pattern is persistent rather than a single storm artifact. Net: real and site-specific, but the entire consequence is truck rolls and monitoring blind spots, roughly 30 labor hours across 13 WOs over ~24 months with zero attributed generation loss, which does not justify a capital or warranty campaign.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Three signals point at a genuine physical layer rather than pure alarm noise: two members were cleared by reseating daisy-chain connections (WO-2025-01128, WO-2026-00042, the latter noting 'second one on that zone this month'), lightning destroyed a surge card and left monitoring only partially restored (WO-2025-00372, which also references a prior strike on the far side of the site), and control WO-2024-00178 ties a mass B06 dropout to a humid, foggy night - consistent with moisture ingress at comms terminations. Five members closed as 'recurring', so the event stream is not decaying. Also, WO-2025-00793 lists 'comms module x4' in parts_used while its narrative says no action was taken, which is a data-integrity inconsistency that could be masking real hardware consumption.

population_at_risk.description: 13 distinct assets at Coralito Flats that have logged a self-clearing comms dropout (tracker zone controllers TR-Z01/Z04/Z07, row TCUs in B03/B05/B06, string inverters in B01/B03/B06, and block B07 comms), plus the blocks referenced in blanket logs; the affected physical population is the site's comms/daisy-chain network, not a discrete equipment fleet.
population_at_risk.basis: Count of unique asset_ids across the 13 cluster members; no installed_base was provided, so the true number of exposed comms nodes cannot be derived.

verdict.recommended_action: Apply a dwell/de-bounce timer and auto-clear rule to Coralito Flats comms alarms so self-restoring dropouts under a set duration log to the historian instead of dispatching a truck, and fold a one-pass daisy-chain and termination inspection of B01/B03/B05/B06 plus the surge protection at B07 into the next scheduled PM sweep.
verdict.business_headline: Coralito Flats generates roughly 3.7x the fleet rate of comms-loss work orders, but every one closed with the asset producing normally and no MWh lost - this is an alarm-configuration and truck-roll problem worth about 30 labor hours over two years, not an equipment failure worth a campaign.

hypotheses.statement: KVP-3600 inverters carry a cooling/fan-control or thermal-threshold defect (likely firmware-set derate point, not blocked airflow) that causes an unlogged 10-12% afternoon power limit at high ambient, and it is progressive/recurring on the same units regardless of fan or filter replacement.
predictions: Repeat WOs on the same asset IDs across separate seasons (e.g. KVP36-2419B-0361 appears in 2024-09 and 2025-07); recurrence flag true on a majority of members.

Members where parts were actually consumed ('cooling fan x3', 'air filter set') generate a follow-up thermal_derate WO on the same asset within the next hot season, i.e. no measurable benefit_pct anywhere in the cluster.
Resolution codes stay in the ESCALATED / VENDOR-REFERRED / NO-FAULT-FOUND family with outcome 'pending' or 'no_change'; essentially zero 'REPAIRED' closures.
Affected units share a serial/build band or firmware revision field; unaffected KVP-3600s in the same cohort at equally hot sites cluster in a different band.
Cluster count grows year-over-year (1 in 2024, 3 in 2025, 3 in 2026 by June) faster than cohort growth.
discriminating_evidence: A firmware/serial field that splits the 7 affected units from the ~369 unaffected ones at comparable site temperature separates H1 from H3/H4.
If any unit was fully repaired (fan controller or board swap) and then produced no further thermal_derate WO in the following summer, H1 is supported and H3 (as-designed behaviour) is weakened.
If peer-model inverters at the SAME sites also log afternoon derate WOs on the same dates, H1 loses to H4.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is largely a text/extraction artifact: several narratives are verbatim or near-verbatim copies of one another and three of seven come from a single technician, so 'thermal_derate' is a labelling convention applied to KVP units rather than a distinct physical event population.
predictions: String-similarity check finds byte-identical or >95% identical narrative bodies across WO-2024-00163 / WO-2025-00720 and across WO-2025-00688 / WO-2025-00908 / WO-2026-00571 / WO-2026-00586.
Author concentration: TECH-0103 authors 3/7 members; the whole cluster is written by <=6 distinct techs out of the site technician population.

Peer models show non-zero counts of a semantically equivalent symptom under a different key (e.g. 'low_output', 'underperformance', 'high_temp'), so the peer_median_rate of 0.0 is a taxonomy artifact rather than a real absence.
Component field is internally inconsistent (one member tagged 'string_inverter', the rest 'central_inverter') for the same model, indicating field-fill noise.
Environment tags split between 'high_ambient_heat' and 'none_mentioned' on narratives describing the same afternoon-heat scenario.
discriminating_evidence: Run exact-duplicate detection on narrative text: if the templated WOs are removed, does n drop below ~4 and the rate become indistinguishable from peers?
Re-map peer-model symptom keys onto a common vocabulary; if peer rate rises to ~0.015-0.02, the lift disappears and H2 explains the candidate without any defect.
Rate of thermal_derate per technician-authored WO: if it is flat across techs, H2 weakens; if it is driven by one or two authors, H2 is favoured.

hypotheses.statement: This is the inverter's designed high-ambient protection operating normally — cabinet temperature rises through the afternoon and recovers after sundown with no stored fault — and the WOs reflect operator unfamiliarity rather than a failure.
predictions: Derate magnitude is tightly clustered (10-12% reported in every narrative) rather than dispersed or worsening, consistent with a fixed spec curve.
Every event self-resolves after sundown with no intervention; no member shows a hard trip, no fault code stored, no parts required to restore output.
Total lost energy is small and bounded: 20.4 MWh over 7 events (~2.9 MWh each), of the order of a few afternoon hours of partial curtailment, not an outage.
All members fall in the hot half of the year (June-September) with none in October-May.
Inspection-only actions ('all six fans turning, filters and plenum clear') find no physical fault in the units that were thoroughly checked.
discriminating_evidence: Compare cabinet-temperature-vs-output on an affected unit against a healthy same-model unit at the same site and hour: if both derate identically, H3 holds and H1 falls.
Check DC:AC ratio / nameplate loading at the affected positions — if derating units are systematically the most heavily loaded, H3 is supported.
If any unit derates at ambient temperatures well below the published operating envelope, H3 is falsified in favour of H1.

hypotheses.statement: Ordinary variation plus discrete summer heat events: 7 events in 376 units (1.9% over ~2 years) is an unremarkable rate, and the apparent model specificity comes from KVP-3600 being concentrated at the hottest sites (Bitter Draw, Ashvale Dry Lake, Joshua Fork) rather than from any model property.
predictions: Member dates concentrate on a small number of calendar days/weeks that coincide with site-wide heat-related WO spikes across all asset classes (tracker, transformer, comms).
Site mix of the KVP-3600 cohort is skewed toward desert/high-ambient sites relative to peer-model cohorts; peer models with zero thermal_derate WOs are installed predominantly at cooler sites.
After stratifying by site (or by site-season), the KVP-3600 thermal_derate rate falls within the range of same-site peer models.
No single asset dominates: excluding the one repeat asset, the remaining events are one-per-unit and spread across 4 sites.
Poisson expectation for 376 units over the observation window makes 7 events unsurprising; comparable clusters of n=5-8 exist for other model-symptom pairs with equally 'null' lift.
discriminating_evidence: Site-stratified rate comparison: if same-site peer models also show ~2% thermal derate, H4 explains everything and H1 is unnecessary.
If the cluster spans many independent hot days across three summers rather than 2-3 discrete heat waves, the 'discrete weather event' part of H4 weakens.
If KVP-3600 units at cool-climate sites also produce thermal_derate WOs, H4 falls and H1 or H3 is favoured.

verdict.reasoning: H2 (text artifact) does not survive the control set: the controls are templated in exactly the same way — WO-2025-00179 and WO-2026-00286 are near-identical overcurrent narratives, and WO-2025-00770 and WO-2025-00465 are near-identical undervoltage narratives — so verbatim phrasing is a corpus-wide narration habit, not evidence that these seven events are one event double-counted; the members carry six distinct asset IDs across four sites and three summers, so they are distinct physical events. H4 is weakened because one member sits at coastal Tidemarsh Bay (WO-2025-00720), not only at the desert sites. What the members actually describe, however, is textbook designed high-ambient protection: a tightly clustered 10-12% afternoon limit, no stored fault and nothing to reset (WO-2025-00670), and the fullest inspection in the set found filters, intake screens and plenum clear with all six fans turning and cabinet temperature recovering after sundown unaided (WO-2026-00586) — H3's signature. H1 cannot be excluded (KVP36-2419B-0361 recurred in WO-2024-00163 and WO-2025-00688, and fans/filters were consumed in WO-2025-00908 and WO-2026-00571 with no recorded benefit), but nothing here shows derate occurring below the published operating envelope, and the affected serials (2419B, 2420B, 2426B, 2427C, 2428C, 2436C) overlap the same bands as non-derating control units (KVP36-2420B-0350, KVP36-2420B-0355, KVP36-2421B-0201). Impact is small and bounded — partial afternoon curtailment on 6 of 376 units over roughly two years, 28.5 labour hours total, no outages and no hard trips — so this does not warrant commercial action now.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Three signals argue for a real model defect rather than designed behaviour: KVP36-2419B-0361 recurred across two separate seasons (WO-2024-00163, WO-2025-00688); parts were consumed with no recorded improvement (cooling fan x3 in WO-2025-00908, air filter set in WO-2026-00571); and every OEM case remains pending (WO-2025-00688, WO-2025-00908, WO-2026-00571, WO-2026-00586) rather than closed as normal operation. A same-model unit also logged unexplained low airflow with clean filters and all fans running (WO-2025-00920), hinting at a cooling-control issue the current data cannot resolve. If Kelvara confirms the derate setpoint activates below the published ambient envelope, this flips to a warranty-grade H1 finding.

population_at_risk.description: Six distinct KVP-3600 assets observed exhibiting afternoon thermal derate (KVP36-2419B-0361, KVP36-2436C-0275, KVP36-2426B-0289, KVP36-2428C-0169, KVP36-2420B-0352, KVP36-2427C-0381) out of a 376-unit KVP-3600 installed base; fleet-wide exposure would only apply if a common firmware setpoint is confirmed, which this data does not establish.
population_at_risk.basis: Distinct asset_ids appearing in the seven cluster member work orders, against total_installed for KVP-3600 in installed_base.

verdict.recommended_action: Consolidate the four open Kelvara cases (WO-2025-00688, WO-2025-00908, WO-2026-00571, WO-2026-00586) into a single vendor query for the KVP-3600 published derate curve and firmware thermal setpoint, and track afternoon derate MWh on the six named assets through the next hot season — re-open as a warranty claim only if derate is confirmed below the published ambient envelope or event count grows.
verdict.business_headline: Seven afternoon derate tickets on KVP-3600 inverters look like the units' own high-ambient protection working as designed — 6 of 376 units, self-recovering, no outages — so hold at monitoring until Kelvara confirms the derate setpoint against spec.

hypotheses.statement: A specific cooling-fan bearing lot or fan-bank design in the KVP-3600 cooling package is failing prematurely, concentrated in a contiguous build range (serial blocks 24xxB/24xxC) and firmware 4.2.x units, producing repeatable two-fan replacements.
predictions: The 7 affected asset_ids should cluster in a narrow serial/build-code band (2418–2436) while the ~369 unaffected KVP-3600 units include many serials outside that band, i.e. the failure rate within the band is materially higher than outside it.
The failing fans should occupy the same position(s) in the bank across work orders ('two fans', 'others tested ok' each time), not random positions.
Follow-up work orders on the same asset_ids should show additional fan replacements within 12–24 months as the remaining original fans from the same lot fail.

Time-since-commissioning (or time since first energisation, if derivable from asset records or first PM WO) should be similar across the 7 events, indicating a common wear-out age rather than random incidence.
Parts-issue records should show cooling fans drawn against KVP-3600 assets at a higher per-unit rate than against peer inverter models over the same window.
discriminating_evidence: Serial/build-code concentration: if failures are spread uniformly across the whole KVP-3600 serial range, a lot defect is disfavoured and H2/H3 rise.
Repeat replacements on the same asset within the corpus window (supports defect, argues against one-time end-of-life wear).
Whether peer models, when their narratives are text-searched for 'fan' and 'bearing', show comparable per-unit fan replacement rates under a different symptom label (would move weight to H3).

hypotheses.statement: Cooling fans are a consumable and 7 replacements across 376 units over an ~11-month window (~1.9%, roughly 2%/yr) is ordinary end-of-life bearing wear that would be unremarkable in any inverter fleet of this age.
predictions: All 7 events resolve on first visit with no recurrence flag set (already true in the sample) and no associated derate/trip or thermal fault work orders preceding them.
Events should be spread roughly evenly in time (Jul-25, Sep-25 x2, Apr-26, May-26, Jun-26 x2) rather than bunched into a single month or a single commissioning cohort.
Events should be spread across many distinct sites and techs (7 WOs across 6 sites in the sample) rather than concentrated at one site.
Reported energy loss should be small and mostly incidental (16.0 MWh over 7 WOs, ~2.3 MWh each), consistent with brief planned outages rather than failure-driven downtime.
Peer models with comparable installed base and age should show non-zero fan-related work orders somewhere in the corpus, even if coded to a different symptom.
discriminating_evidence: Normalise by unit-years rather than units: if KVP-3600 has been installed longer than peers, an age-matched rate comparison should collapse the apparent excess.
Compare KVP-3600 fan replacements per unit-year against the OEM-agnostic fleet-wide fan replacement rate computed from all narratives mentioning fans; parity supports H2.
Absence of any serial-band or firmware concentration (see H1) plus absence of repeat failures would leave H2 as the parsimonious reading.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is a classification artifact: peer models' identical fan-bearing work is being coded to other symptoms (e.g. 'overheating', 'noise', 'abnormal_sound') or captured as PM rather than CM, so the peer median of 0.0 and the null lift reflect label routing, not a real difference in fan failures.
predictions: A free-text search for 'fan' AND ('bearing' OR 'noisy') across ALL models should return work orders on peer models that carry a symptom label other than 'corrosion_or_wear'.

The symptom vocabulary should show that 'corrosion_or_wear' is a broad catch-all; within KVP-3600 it should also absorb non-fan wear items, and the 7 fan WOs should be the only sub-type present, indicating narrow routing rather than genuine specificity.

One member (WO-2026-00578) carries resolution_code 'CLEANED' while the extracted action is 'part_replaced', showing the resolution/symptom fields and the narrative disagree — such field/narrative mismatches should appear at a measurable rate across the corpus.

KVP-3600 may simply be the largest single-model cohort (376 units); if peer cohorts are much smaller, a ~2%/yr event rate would be expected to yield 0 events in most of them purely by population size.
The near-identical narrative strings ('two fans rplcd <asset>, bearings noisy') should recur verbatim, consistent with a template or autofill rather than independent observation.
discriminating_evidence: Peer cohort sizes: if the largest peer cohort is under ~100 units, zero events is the expected outcome at a 2%/yr rate and the 'lift' is meaningless — this alone can retire the candidate.
Finding peer-model fan/bearing narratives under a different symptom label directly falsifies the 'peer median 0.0' premise.

Cross-tab of symptom label vs. extracted component across all models: if 'corrosion_or_wear' maps almost exclusively to cooling_fan for one model and to other components for peers, the label is model-dependent and the comparison is invalid.

hypotheses.statement: The pattern is driven by a small group of technicians (TECH-0131 authored 3 of 7) applying a discretionary 'replace both noisy fans and clean the plenum' practice during other visits, so the cluster measures inspection and reporting behaviour rather than a change in fan condition.
predictions: Author concentration: a handful of tech IDs should account for a disproportionate share of the 7 WOs relative to their share of all KVP-3600 work orders.
The same techs should show elevated fan-replacement rates on peer inverter models too, if they service mixed-model sites.
Priorities should skew low and non-urgent (P2/P3 only in the sample, no P1) with no preceding alarm, trip or thermal-derate work order on the same asset in the days before.

Narratives should show the work was bundled with other activity ('cleaned the plenum while I was in there', 'others tested ok'), and labor hours should be modest and variable (2.3–7.9 h) rather than reflecting a dedicated failure response.
Sites serviced primarily by techs who do NOT use this practice should show zero KVP-3600 fan work orders despite similar unit counts and ages.
discriminating_evidence: Tech-level rate normalisation: if fan replacement rate per KVP-3600 unit serviced is flat across techs, H4 is disfavoured and H1/H2 gain.
Presence or absence of a preceding fault/alarm WO on the same asset — objective triggers argue for real failure (H1/H2), no trigger argues for discretionary replacement (H4).
Whether the same techs replace fans on peer models at similar rates; if they do, the model attribution in the candidate key is spurious.

verdict.reasoning: The seven members are routine, low-priority, first-visit-resolved replacements of two fans out of a multi-fan bank with 'bearings noisy' as the only finding (WO-2025-00674, WO-2025-00840, WO-2025-00872, WO-2026-00433, WO-2026-00469, WO-2026-00578, WO-2026-00622) — 7 events across 376 units in ~11 months, roughly 2%/yr, which is ordinary consumable turnover for cooling fans. The controls falsify the key premises of the defect and reporting-culture readings: the same failure mode (seized fan, bearing gone) appears on a 2016-build unit under a different symptom label (WO-2025-00631, cooling_airflow_low) and fan-bank work also lands under wildlife_intrusion (WO-2025-01005), so 'corrosion_or_wear' is one routing path among several rather than a model-specific signal — this also explains the peer median of 0.0 and the null lift (H3 is directionally right but is a labelling nuance, not an actionable finding). H1 is weak because the affected serials (2418B–2436C) sit inside the same 2024 build band as controls with entirely unrelated failures (WO-2026-00579, WO-2026-00627, WO-2026-00626), i.e. the band is simply where most of the fleet was built (179 of 376 units in 2024), and the one clearly bearing-driven fan failure in the controls is an eight-year-old unit. H4 is partially supported by TECH-0131 authoring 3 of 7 and by the bundled 'cleaned the plenum while I was in there' phrasing, but five distinct techs across six sites over eleven months is too dispersed to be a single crew's practice. No member had a preceding thermal trip attributable to fan loss; the one thermal precursor on an affected asset was blocked filters in high ambient (WO-2025-01068), a different mechanism.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: All seven events fall on 2024-build units (manufacture weeks 18–36, a pool of ~74 units) while ~197 older units generated no 'corrosion_or_wear' fan work in the window; if the older-fleet fan failures visible under other labels (WO-2025-00631) turn out to be rare, an early-life bearing issue in the 2024 build cannot be fully excluded. hypotheses.statement: A discrete build lot of KVP-3600 units (serial block 'KVP36-2432C-xxxx' and neighbouring 24xx blocks) carries a defective IGBT/gate-driver power stage, and this lot alone accounts for the excess hard_fault rate over the peer median.
predictions: Cluster members concentrate disproportionately in a narrow asset_id serial range (24xxC, serials 0354-0379) relative to that range's share of the 376-unit cohort; KVP-3600 units outside that block should sit at or near the 0.018 peer-median rate.

Within the suspect block, failures should be dominated by parts_used containing 'IGBT module' or 'gate driver' and resolution codes PART-REPL / VENDOR-REFERRED / ESCALATED, not RESET or NO-FAULT-FOUND.

hypotheses.statement: The lift is ordinary variation surfaced by multiple comparisons: 17 events against roughly 7 expected over a ~2.5-year window and 376 units is a small absolute excess that would be expected to appear in at least one model-symptom pair when many such pairs are scanned.

Other symptoms for KVP-3600 should show lifts scattered both above and below 1.0 rather than uniformly elevated.

discriminating_evidence: Exact Poisson test on 17 observed versus expected-from-peer-rate exposure, then a multiplicity correction across all evaluated candidates; a corrected p that stays small refutes this hypothesis.
Hold-out test on a later time slice: if the KVP-3600 hard_fault rate reverts toward 0.018 in the next reporting period with no intervention, chance is the better explanation than H1.
Serial-block concentration test (same test as H1): strong concentration is inconsistent with random variation.

verdict.reasoning: Decoding the asset_id (yyww block, confirmed by WO-2025-00543 where KVP36-1646D is described in-narrative as a 2016 build) shows a sharp step change rather than a model-wide effect: three distinct units from the 2024 week-32 build block (KVP36-2432C-0354, -0356, -0357) suffered IGBT power-stage failures at three different sites within 24 days (WO-2026-00626, WO-2026-00677, WO-2026-00680), each opened as a Kelvara warranty case and each authorised for a no-charge swap — exactly H1's predicted pattern of common build date plus common time-in-service, and inconsistent with H4's random-variation expectation of no block or calendar concentration. That block holds only 8 installed units (units_by_2024_manufacture_week, week 32), so three failures is not ordinary wear. H2 is partly right and is why confidence is not high: five members (WO-2024-00188, WO-2024-00195, WO-2025-00684, WO-2025-00695, WO-2025-00722) are self-clearing nuisance trips closed by RESET/NO-FAULT-FOUND with 1.8-3.3 h labour and no parts, and the controls show the same reset-and-hold behaviour on peer hardware (WO-2026-00034, WO-2025-00858, WO-2025-01192) — that slice is ordinary and should be stripped from the rate, but stripping it does not remove the 2432C IGBT trio. H3 is supported only as a data-quality defect, not as a rate explanation: parts_used is plainly wrong on several members (WO-2026-00677 and WO-2026-00680 read 'cooling fan' against narratives describing IGBT failures; WO-2025-00636 reads 'IGBT module' against a fan replacement), which corrupts parts analytics but does not manufacture three OEM-authorised IGBT claims out of one build week.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: The lot signal rests on three events from three units, and one of those units (KVP36-2432C-0354) had previously produced only a benign self-clearing trip (WO-2025-00722). Roughly a third of the cluster is nuisance-trip resets indistinguishable from the controls, so the headline 2.51x lift overstates the hardware problem. 2024-build units are about half the installed base and are still in warranty, which independently raises formal work-order generation (H3), so some of the 24xx concentration is reporting behaviour. Structured parts_used fields for this model are demonstrably unreliable, so any parts-based confirmation must come from the OEM case records, not the CMMS.

hypotheses.statement: A genuine structural defect exists in a subset of Sundowner Mesa rows — torque-tube/bearing misalignment at or near the third bearing in blocks B02 and B05 — driven by a common foundation-settlement or bearing/damper batch issue, and it is distinct from the generic controller recalibrations in the same cluster.
predictions: The structural subset (component=tracker_structure, parts: damper/bearing housing/coupling) should be spatially concentrated: asset_ids clustered in B02/B05 and in adjacent row numbers (e.g. R057/R058), not uniformly spread across B01–B08.

Repeat or follow-on work orders should appear on the same or neighbouring rows within 6–12 months, even if the 'recurrence' flag is currently false (check asset_id reappearance across all symptoms, not just tracker_misalignment).
Structural cases should carry systematically higher labor_hours and parts consumption than controller cases (3.8 vs 1.7 h is the wrong direction here — needs to hold across the full population).
Other symptoms on the same assets (e.g. tracker_stall, abnormal_noise, motor_overcurrent) should be elevated at Sundowner Mesa relative to fleet, since a bent torque tube loads the drive train.
If foundation-related, commissioning-era or PM work orders on those rows should mention pier, grout, or level checks.
discriminating_evidence: Asset-level geographic clustering: if the 7 WOs map to a contiguous block/row band, defect is favoured; if scattered evenly across blocks, artifact/noise is favoured.
Recurrence on the same asset_id after 'resolved' closure — a real structural defect should not stay fixed by shimming.
Presence of the same 'third bearing' language on assets handled by techs other than TECH-0231; if the phrase only ever appears from one tech, it is a phrasing artifact rather than a physical finding.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is largely a reporting/logging artifact: one technician (TECH-0231, 5 of 7 WOs) uses copy-pasted narrative templates and a loose 'tracker_misalignment' label, inflating Sundowner Mesa's count for a symptom other sites log under different symptom codes or as routine PM.
predictions: Verbatim-identical narrative strings should recur across distinct asset_ids (already visible: three WOs share 'torque tube out of true at the third bearing. Shimmed and realigned.' on TR-B05-R024, TR-B02-R072, TR-B02-R057).
Removing TECH-0231's work orders should drop Sundowner Mesa's tracker_misalignment rate to near or below the fleet rate of 0.39/GW-month.
TECH-0231 should show above-average use of the tracker_misalignment code across every site they have worked, not just Sundowner Mesa.
Other sites should show a compensating excess in adjacent symptom codes (tracker_stall, tracker_no_response, controller_fault) such that the combined tracker-symptom rate is comparable fleet-wide.

Field inconsistency should be widespread in this tech's records: resolution_code=PART-REPL with empty parts_used (WO-2025-01179, WO-2026-00073 pattern), or RESET/ADJUSTED codes paired with hardware parts.
discriminating_evidence: Tech-stratified rate: compute tracker_misalignment per GW-month with and without TECH-0231; a large collapse implicates the reporter, stability implicates the site.
Cross-site behaviour of TECH-0231 and TECH-0194 — if they carry the elevated rate with them to other sites, the site is not the cause.
Fleet-wide count of exact duplicate narrative strings: if templating is uniform across the fleet, it explains labelling but not the 3.4x lift; if concentrated at this site/tech, it explains both.

hypotheses.statement: This is ordinary Poisson variation on a small denominator: 7 events against an expected ~2.1 over only 5.3 GW-months is within the range a fleet-wide multiple-comparisons scan will throw up by chance, possibly compounded by understated exposure for this site.
predictions: The 95% interval on 7 counts is roughly 2.8–14 events, i.e. a rate band of ~0.53–2.7/GW-month, which overlaps or sits close to several other sites' observed rates — other site|symptom candidates in the same scan should show similar lifts at similar n.
The 7 events should be roughly uniform in time (observed: Mar, Apr x2, Aug, Sep, Dec, Jan) with no burst structure — consistent with a homogeneous Poisson process, not a triggered failure wave.
Sundowner Mesa should NOT be elevated across other symptom families; the excess should be confined to this one cell.
If exposure_gw_months is recomputed from actual commissioned capacity and in-service dates, the rate should move materially toward 0.39.
discriminating_evidence: Re-run the scan on a held-out time window (e.g. only 2026 data, or only H1 2025): a chance cluster will not reproduce its lift, a real one will.
Count how many site|symptom cells were tested; if hundreds, a lift of 3.4 at n=7 is expected to occur several times by chance.
Audit the exposure denominator — partial-year energisation or block-level derating would explain the lift with no failure-side cause at all.

hypotheses.statement: Sundowner Mesa is a high-wind, exposed-mesa site, and the misalignment work orders are expected wind-loading wear on dampers, bearings and couplings rather than a defect — normal maintenance whose rate is simply higher at windier sites.
predictions: Wind-related parts (damper, bearing housing, coupling) should dominate parts_used at this site across all symptoms, not just tracker_misalignment.
Event dates should cluster around seasonal high-wind or stow-event periods (spring in the desert Southwest: note Mar/Apr x2 here) with a quieter summer, and stow-related WOs should co-occur.
Other exposed sites in the fleet should show a similar tracker_misalignment lift, so the fleet rate should be bimodal by site exposure rather than Sundowner Mesa being a lone outlier.
Narratives at this site should mention wind, stow, gust, or dust in the environment field at above-fleet frequency — currently ALL seven are 'none_mentioned', which counts against this hypothesis.
discriminating_evidence: The environment extraction field: seven of seven 'none_mentioned' is direct evidence against a weather driver, unless extraction is known to under-capture environment mentions — test extraction recall on a labelled sample.
Temporal correlation between misalignment WOs and site stow/high-wind alarm events in the same work-order stream.
Compare Sundowner Mesa's rate against other sites sharing the same tracker OEM and terrain class; if only this site is elevated, environment is not sufficient.

verdict.reasoning: The apparent physical signature that made this cluster interesting — the verbatim string 'torque tube out of true at the third bearing. Shimmed and realigned.' on three different assets (WO-2025-00227, WO-2025-00324, WO-2025-00350) — appears in the controls as the same kind of template, not as a finding: 'purlin bent on the north end. Straightened, torqued, verified travel' repeats across WO-2025-00268 and WO-2025-00223, 'stow pin damaged. Replaced the pin and checked the adjacent bays' across WO-2025-00284 and WO-2025-00285, and 'limit switch bracket bent. Reformed the bracket and recalibrated the row' across WO-2025-00339 and WO-2025-00302. Templating and loose coding are therefore site-wide behaviour, not evidence of a shared bearing/foundation defect, which defeats H1. The controls also supply an alternative driver for the spring subset: WO-2025-00240 documents a 71 mph microburst on 2025-03-14 with rows caught partway to stow and bent dampers/twisted torque tubes, and WO-2025-00258 and WO-2025-00368 are explicit post-event cleanup — the March/April misalignment WOs sit directly in that cleanup window, making them a discrete weather event rather than a systemic defect. The remaining four members (WO-2025-00754, WO-2025-00930, WO-2025-01179, WO-2026-00073) are generic limit recalibrations scattered across B01, B05 and B08 with no spatial concentration, no recurrence, and in two cases no parts at all. At n=7 on 5.3 GW-months, with a mixed and templated composition, this does not survive as a systemic finding; H3's small-denominator argument also remains fully live and I cannot rule it out from what I was shown.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Three of the structural members do sit in B02/B05 on nearby rows (R057, R058, R072, R024) and carry damper/bearing-housing/coupling parts, so a localised bearing or foundation issue cannot be formally excluded without asset-level layout data or a recurrence check on those rows. All seven members also extract environment as 'none_mentioned', so the microburst link is inferred from date proximity to WO-2025-00240 rather than stated in the member narratives. Tech-stratified rates were not available to test H2's central prediction directly.

verdict.recommended_action: Close this as non-systemic and instead route Sundowner Mesa's work-order records to data governance to stop narrative templating and fix resolution_code/parts mismatches (e.g. WO-2025-01179 coded PART-REPL with no parts, WO-2026-00073 coded NO-FAULT-FOUND yet 7.0 labor hours and outcome 'resolved', WO-2025-00240 coded RESET with 'tracker motor x4').
verdict.business_headline: Sundowner Mesa's 3.4x tracker-misalignment lift is a copy-paste narrative and mis-coding artifact layered on top of March 2025 microburst cleanup, not a tracker defect — no warranty or remediation exposure, but the site's work-order data quality is degrading fleet analytics.

hypotheses.statement: There is no KVP-3600-specific ground-fault problem: 33 events across 376 units (0.088/unit vs peer median 0.080, lift 1.1) is ordinary variation in a generic, high-frequency symptom that every inverter model in the fleet reports at a similar rate.
predictions: Ranking all model|symptom pairs, ground_fault appears in the top few symptoms for most models, not just KVP-3600.
A binomial/Poisson interval on 33/376 overlaps the peer median rate (0.08); the excess is ~3 work orders over 2.5+ years.
Per-unit ground-fault counts are near-Poisson: mostly 0, a few 1, essentially no units with 3+ repeats (recurrence=false throughout).
Mean labor_hours (5.1) and lost MWh per event for KVP-3600 ground faults are within the fleet distribution for the same symptom on other models.
Events are spread thinly across many sites (12+ sites in a 14-record sample) with no site contributing a disproportionate share after normalising by units installed.
discriminating_evidence: Compute rate per unit-year rather than per unit; if KVP-3600 fleet age or commissioning date is similar to peers and the rate still sits at ~1.1x, the signal dies.
If instead a specific serial block or site shows 3-5x the fleet rate, H1 is falsified in favour of H2.
If ground_fault rate for KVP-3600 exceeds peers only in one calendar quarter, H1 loses to H4/environmental.

hypotheses.statement: A real but installation-side defect exists: DC home runs and string connectors at combiner boxes are being chafed or pinched (rack uprights, gland entries), producing genuine earth faults concentrated in specific combiner positions, sites, or install vintages rather than in the KVP-3600 inverter itself.
predictions: Roughly half or more of the 33 narratives name a physical cause at a combiner (CB-Bxx-yy) — chafed home run or pinched connector — and close with repaired_in_place or part_replaced.
The named combiner IDs cluster in a limited set of positions/rows rather than being uniform across all CB numbers at a site.
The same physical-cause narratives should appear on non-KVP models at sites built by the same EPC/installer, i.e. the pattern tracks site/vintage, not model.
Asset-ID vintage digits (e.g. 16xx/17xx vs 24xx) should show a skew: one build era carries a disproportionate share of chafe/pinch findings.
Physical-cause events should have higher labor_hours and higher lost_mwh than the reset-only events in the same cluster.
discriminating_evidence: Cross-tab cause-type (physical vs no-fault-found) against site and installer/vintage: if physical causes concentrate in a few sites shared with other inverter models, the defect is racking/harness, not KVP-3600.
If chafe/pinch findings are evenly distributed across all sites and vintages at background rate, H2 collapses back to H1.
Repeat ground faults on the same asset_id or same combiner ID would strongly support an unresolved systemic routing defect.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is partly a bookkeeping artifact: resolution_code, narrative text, and NLP-extracted fields contradict each other (RESET codes on connector replacements, NO-FAULT-FOUND codes on part replacements, 'central_inverter'/'string_inverter' component tags on string-walk jobs), so the 33 records do not represent one coherent failure mode and may include templated or duplicated entries.
predictions: A direct cross-tab of resolution_code against extracted.action shows disagreement in a large fraction of the 33 records (e.g. RESET paired with part_replaced, NO-FAULT-FOUND paired with part_replaced).
Several narratives are near-verbatim copies differing only in asset_id and combiner ID ('tripped on DC GF. Traced it to a pinched connector in CB-...'), indicating template or copy-paste entry.
parts_used is blank on most records that the narrative says had a connector replaced — parts consumption does not corroborate the stated repairs.
extracted.component disagrees with the component named in the narrative in a measurable share of records (inverter tagged where only strings/combiners were touched).
The same code/narrative disagreement rate appears for other models' ground-fault records, showing it is a corpus-wide coding hygiene issue, not KVP-specific.
discriminating_evidence: Split the 33 into (a) narrative-confirmed physical fault and (b) reset-only/no-fault-found; if the split is roughly even, the 'cluster' is two populations and its rate should be recomputed per sub-population before any lift claim.
If parts inventory issuance records match the claimed connector replacements, the narratives are trustworthy and H3 weakens.
If duplicate-text detection finds identical narratives on distinct assets and dates, at least part of the count is template noise.

hypotheses.statement: The no-fault-found subset (walked strings, meggered OK, reset held) is nuisance tripping from transient insulation leakage — morning dew, humidity, or high-ambient-heat conditions pushing leakage past the detector threshold — not a hardware defect, and it inflates the ground_fault count without any physical failure.
predictions: A substantial subset of the 33 records carry resolution_code NO-FAULT-FOUND or RESET with action reset_or_restart, outcome resolved, recurrence false, and blank parts_used.
These reset-only events cluster by date/season or by narrow date windows shared across multiple sites (several assets tripping within the same few days).
Reset-only events have low lost_mwh and shorter downtime than physical-cause events, since restoration is immediate after reset.
environment tags of high_ambient_heat or moisture-related terms should appear more often in reset-only records than in chafe/pinch records if the trigger is climatic.
Peer inverter models at the same sites should show a matching burst of reset-only ground faults on the same dates.
discriminating_evidence: Plot event dates for reset-only vs physical-cause subsets: temporal clustering in the former plus a flat distribution in the latter separates H4 from H2.
If reset-only ground faults on the same dates also hit non-KVP models at the same sites, the driver is environmental/site-wide, not model-specific.
If reset-only events are uniformly distributed year-round and show no cross-site coincidence, H4 fails and the resets are better explained by H3 (mis-coding) or H1.

verdict.reasoning: The claimed signal is 0.088 events/unit against a peer median of 0.080 (lift 1.1) — roughly three excess work orders across 376 units over ~2.5 years, which is ordinary variation, and the narrative content gives no reason to override that. The two physical failure modes in the members — home runs chafed against rack uprights (WO-2024-00002, WO-2024-00063, WO-2026-00081, WO-2026-00536, WO-2025-00373) and pinched connectors at combiners (WO-2024-00338, WO-2025-00158, WO-2025-01045, WO-2025-01105, WO-2026-00049) — appear verbatim on non-KVP hardware in the controls: CES40 at Coralito Flats (WO-2025-00506) and CES40 at Hollowell Ranch (WO-2025-00963) have literally the same 'dc gf, pinched connector cb-..., rplcd' text, and SLT25 at Blackfoot Draw (WO-2026-00087) shows the damp-morning nuisance trip. That kills the model-specific framing: whatever DC-side chafe/pinch exposure exists tracks site, racking and cable management (see also controls WO-2025-00163 cable sag/clip failures, WO-2024-00053 and WO-2025-00416 home runs sitting low in mow rows), not the KVP-3600 inverter, so H2's mechanism may be real but does not belong to this candidate. H3 has real support as a secondary effect — resolution codes contradict the narratives in a large share of members (WO-2025-00158 coded RESET on a connector replacement, WO-2024-00338 and WO-2025-00524 coded NO-FAULT-FOUND on part replacements, WO-2025-01192 coded RESET with a string connector booked against a nothing-found string walk) and several narratives are near-verbatim duplicates across different sites and vintages — which means the 33 records are not one coherent failure mode and the 1.1 lift is, if anything, overstated. H4's reset-only subset (WO-2025-00096, WO-2025-00378, WO-2025-00460, WO-2025-01147, WO-2026-00335, WO-2026-00592) further splits the count into a second population with no hardware finding.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: The physical-cause subset is genuine and non-trivial: home-run chafe against rack steel is a repeatable installation defect with real labor (2.3-8.8 hrs per event), one asset repeated (KVP36-1629C-0260 in WO-2026-00335 and again in WO-2026-00536), and one control (WO-2025-00092 at Pecan Fork) explicitly recommends a row-level campaign for a related enclosure defect. If the fleet is re-cut by site/EPC/racking vintage rather than by inverter model, a genuine escalation may exist there — it just is not a KVP-3600 finding.

population_at_risk.description: No KVP-3600-specific at-risk population is supported; the observed rate is within peer variation and the same failure text appears on CES40 and SLT25 units.
population_at_risk.basis: 33 events / 376 units = 0.088 vs peer median 0.080 implies ~3 excess events fleet-wide over the record window, which is not separable from noise or from the coding/duplication artifacts identified.

verdict.recommended_action: Close this model-level candidate and re-cut the ground-fault population by site, combiner ID and racking/install vintage across all inverter models before any campaign is scoped, and separately fix the resolution-code vs narrative disagreement seen in WO-2025-00158, WO-2024-00338 and WO-2025-01192.
verdict.business_headline: KVP-3600 ground faults are running at the fleet norm (1.1x peer median) and the same chafed-home-run and pinched-connector findings appear on CES40 and SLT25 units at the same sites — this is a cable-management/site issue, not an inverter-model defect, and warrants no warranty or vendor action.
