verdict.contradicting_evidence: Two DC ground faults in adjacent combiner boxes (WO-2025-00671 at CB-B08-17, WO-2026-00050 at CB-B09-14) plus two Kernwood cable-sag inspections (WO-2025-00127, WO-2025-00021) do suggest a genuine but site-local, BOS-scoped wiring/workmanship issue at Kernwood that is worth local attention even though it is unrelated to the MG-3300/17Q4 build. Resolution coding is also unreliable in the members (WO-2025-00671 closed NO-FAULT-FOUND after a repair; WO-2026-00050 closed RESET after a connector replacement; WO-2025-01227 lists a DC bus capacitor while the narrative says AC contactor; WO-2025-00193 lists IGBT modules while the narrative says control board), so any future re-test of this cohort should use narrative-derived fields rather than coded ones.

population_at_risk.description: No manufacturing-attributable population identified; the 18-unit 17Q4 cohort shows per-asset incidence at the peer median once repeat visits are collapsed.
population_at_risk.basis: 5 distinct asset_ids across the 9 member WOs divided by 18 units in cohort = 0.28/unit, equal to the stated peer median of 0.28.

verdict.recommended_action: Close the MG-3300/17Q4 cohort as not a build defect, and instead hand the two adjacent combiner-box conductor faults (WO-2025-00671, WO-2026-00050) and the open cable-sag walkdown items to the Kernwood site lead as a local BOS inspection task.
verdict.business_headline: The MG-3300 17Q4 'cohort' is an artifact of six repeat visits on two Kernwood assets — per-asset failure rate is at the fleet median and every failure mode also appears at other sites, so there is no warranty case here.

hypotheses.statement: There is no single Birch Coulee comms problem: the 7 work orders are a heterogeneous grab-bag (3 tracker-controller power-cycles, 2 fiber-run failures, 1 RTU reboot, 1 lightning surge) whose count is within ordinary Poisson variation for 4.2 GW-months (expected ~4.0, observed 7, one-sided p roughly 0.1), so the 1.75x lift is a small-numbers artifact of a coarse symptom label.
predictions: Splitting the cluster by extracted.component yields no sub-group with n>=3 that is itself significantly above its own fleet component rate.

Other sites with similar or smaller exposure show comms_loss rates scattered both above and below 0.95/GW-month with comparable lifts (i.e. Birch Coulee is not an outlier in a per-site rate distribution).
The 7 events are spread across ~20 months with no month containing more than 2, and across at least 4 distinct assets/blocks with little repetition.
Recurrence flags are false on all members and resolution codes are dominated by NO-FAULT-FOUND, consistent with unrelated one-off calls.
discriminating_evidence: Recomputing the rate with an exact Poisson confidence interval: if the lower bound sits below the fleet rate of 0.95, this hypothesis survives and the others must explain a signal that statistics cannot confirm.
If any single component sub-group (e.g. fiber/scada_or_comms) shows a rate several times the fleet component rate with repeat assets, H1 is weakened in favour of H2.
If comms_loss counts at this site keep accruing at >1.5/GW-month over the next 6-12 months of exposure, random variation becomes untenable.

hypotheses.statement: The buried/aerial fiber plant between the inverter skids and the blocks at Birch Coulee is degrading site-wide (moisture ingress, rodent damage or poor terminations), producing repeat 'tested bad, patched onto the spare pair' events (B02, B08) that have already consumed the redundant pairs and will recur as hard SCADA outages.
predictions: More than one work order narrative at this site contains fiber/spare-pair language, with distinct block IDs, and at least one carries an unclosed follow-up ('needs permanent fix scheduling') that has no corresponding completed PM/CM record.
Future comms_loss work orders on blocks already patched onto spare pairs will show longer labor hours and escalate in priority (P1/P2) because no redundancy remains.
Fiber-related comms_loss at this site is confined to scada_or_comms component and block-level assets (B0x), not to tracker controllers.
Other sites of the same vintage/EPC show a comparable share of fiber-run failures if the defect is a build-quality issue, or do not if it is local to Birch Coulee.
discriminating_evidence: An OTDR/splice-record or parts trail (fiber, patch panels, media converters) attached to Birch Coulee work orders that is absent at peer sites.
Repeat comms_loss on the same block ID after a spare-pair patch would confirm progressive plant degradation rather than two coincidental cable faults.
If the two fiber narratives turn out to be near-duplicate text on the same physical run (B02 vs B08 mislabelled), this collapses into H1's duplicate/templating artifact.

hypotheses.statement: The tracker-controller subset is benign nuisance behaviour: TCUs intermittently drop off the tracker comms bus and are cleared by a power cycle with no fault found and no lost production, i.e. an expected firmware/RS-485 housekeeping issue being logged as a corrective work order rather than a real failure.
predictions: All tracker_controller members have resolution_code NO-FAULT-FOUND or PART-REPL with no parts actually consumed, action = reset_or_restart, outcome = resolved, and low labor hours (<5).
Reported lost MWh attributable to the tracker_controller members is near zero, with the bulk of the 63.8 MWh sitting in the lightning and SCADA/fiber events.
The same reset-only TCU pattern appears at other sites with the same tracker vendor, at a rate that explains part of the fleet baseline.
No TCU replacement parts appear in the parts_used field for any of these events.
discriminating_evidence: Per-member lost_mwh and parts_used breakdown: if the TCU events carry material energy loss or genuine part replacements, they are not benign.
Repeat offences on the same TR-xxx asset ID would indicate a real hardware/wiring defect rather than random bus dropouts.
Whether the TCU dropout rate at Birch Coulee exceeds the same-vendor tracker fleet rate once normalised by tracker count rather than GW.

hypotheses.statement: Birch Coulee's excess is driven by discrete storm/lightning exposure and inadequate surge protection on the comms path, so comms_loss events cluster around convective-season storm dates rather than accruing uniformly.
predictions: Work orders with environment tag storm_or_lightning are over-represented at this site relative to the fleet share of storm-tagged comms_loss.
Event dates concentrate in late summer/spring convective months, and the highest-severity members (P1, ESCALATED, largest labor hours and lost MWh) are the storm-tagged ones.
Surge cards, surge arrestors or grounding-related parts appear in parts_used or narratives at this site more often than fleet average.
Other symptom families at Birch Coulee (e.g. inverter faults) also show storm-date co-occurrence on the same dates as the comms events.
discriminating_evidence: Only 1 of 7 members carries a storm environment tag; if a date-join across all site work orders shows the other 6 are not co-located with storm-tagged events elsewhere on site, H4 is largely falsified.
Repeat surge-component replacements on the same panel/skid would support H4 over H2 (a surge path defect rather than a cable-plant defect).
Seasonal breakdown of the site's comms_loss counts: a flat month-by-month distribution points to H1/H2/H3, a convective-season spike points to H4.

verdict.reasoning: The seven members are a heterogeneous grab-bag rather than one mechanism: three tracker-controller power-cycles with no parts and no fault found (WO-2025-00091, WO-2025-00726, WO-2025-00751), one lightning/surge-card event (WO-2024-00140), one RTU lockup reboot (WO-2026-00211), and two fiber spare-pair patches (WO-2025-00987, WO-2026-00414). Every one of those sub-patterns is reproduced in the matched controls at other sites: the fiber 'tested bad between the skid and the block, patched onto the spare pair, permanent fix needs scheduling' narrative appears near-verbatim at Kernwood Basin (WO-2025-00165), the TCU power-cycle-with-no-root-cause appears at Coralito Flats (WO-2025-00172) and Kernwood Basin (WO-2026-00129), and the overnight RTU lockup/reboot appears at Red Clay Flats (WO-2025-00825). That kills H2 as a Birch-Coulee-specific fiber-plant defect (the same text and same failure mode occur off-site, and the two site members are on different blocks with no repeat on a patched block) and supports H3 only as an explanation of the benign TCU subset, not of the site lift. With 7 observed against ~4 expected over 4.2 GW-months the one-sided Poisson p is roughly 0.1, so the 1.75x lift is not distinguishable from ordinary variation once the coarse symptom label is split by component.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Two Birch Coulee blocks (WO-2025-00987 on B02, WO-2026-00414 on B08) are now running on spare fiber pairs with explicit unclosed follow-ups, and WO-2026-00414 states there is no redundancy left on that run; that is a real deferred-repair exposure even though it is not statistically a site-level outlier and is mirrored at Kernwood Basin (WO-2025-00165). If a third fiber run fails at Birch Coulee, or if a previously patched block (B02/B08) recurs, H2 should be revisited.

population_at_risk.description: Birch Coulee block-to-skid fiber runs currently carried on a spare pair with an unclosed permanent-repair request (B02, B08); one comparable run exists at Kernwood Basin (B04), giving 3 fleet-wide in the data shown.
population_at_risk.basis: Counted directly from narratives of WO-2025-00987 and WO-2026-00414 (plus control WO-2025-00165); total fiber-run population per site is not quantifiable from this data.

verdict.recommended_action: Close the finding as ordinary variation, but open work items to permanently repair the two spare-pair-patched fiber runs at Birch Coulee (B02, B08) and re-check the site rate after another 6-12 months of exposure.
verdict.business_headline: Birch Coulee's comms_loss rate is not a real site defect once split by component and compared against other sites, though two block fiber runs there are running with no spare-pair redundancy and need scheduled permanent repair.

hypotheses.statement: Salt Fork Landing has a systemic tracker comms daisy-chain termination/connector defect (loose or improperly torqued splices at zone controllers) that intermittently drops TCUs and is temporarily cleared by reseating or power cycling.
predictions: A majority of the 7 members resolve as RESET / reseat / NO-FAULT-FOUND with zero or near-zero parts consumption and low labor hours (observed: 5 of 7, mean ~3.5 h, 1 part).

Repeat work orders on the same asset_id or same zone within 60-90 days (already seen on TR-Z03: 'second time on this zone in about two months'); a query of asset_id recurrence at this site should show higher repeat-offender concentration than the fleet.
Affected assets should concentrate in specific zones/blocks (Z01, Z03, Z09, Z11, B03, B07) rather than distributing uniformly across the site's tracker population.
Fleet-wide, sites sharing the same tracker vendor/installer should show elevated comms_loss rates; sites with other tracker vendors should not.
discriminating_evidence: Asset-level recurrence: if the same TCUs/zones recur repeatedly, that favours a physical defect over random noise or a one-off weather event.
Whether events persist into winter/low-storm months at a similar rate — a defect keeps producing tickets year-round, a storm-season driver does not.
Whether definitive repairs (connector replacement, re-termination, PART-REPL) eventually stop recurrence on the offending zones.

hypotheses.statement: The elevated rate is ordinary Poisson variation on a small exposure base: 7 events against ~4.4 expected at the fleet rate over 4.6 GW-months is well within chance, and no site-specific cause exists.
predictions: A Poisson test on n=7 vs expected 4.37 should be non-significant (p roughly 0.15-0.20); the 95% interval on the site rate should overlap the fleet rate of 0.95.

Other sites with similarly small exposure should show comparable or larger lifts in the same corpus, i.e. lift magnitude should be inversely related to exposure_gw_months across all site_symptom candidates.
Splitting the site's window in half should show unstable rates (e.g. 2 events in the first half, 5 in the second) rather than a consistently elevated rate.
No single component, zone, or tech should account for a disproportionate share once the counts are broken down — the 7 events should look heterogeneous in cause and resolution.
discriminating_evidence: Adding another 3-6 months of exposure: under this hypothesis the rate regresses toward 0.95; under H1/H3 it stays elevated or stays seasonally patterned.
Comparing this candidate's lift against the distribution of lifts for all low-exposure site_symptom cells — if 1.62 sits mid-pack, the cluster is unremarkable.
Absence of asset-level repeat concentration would strongly support this over H1.

hypotheses.statement: The apparent cluster is driven by a single convective storm season: lightning and surge transients between June and September 2025 caused most of the comms dropouts, including one confirmed lightning strike that destroyed a surge card.
predictions: Date distribution should be strongly concentrated in Jun-Sep (observed: 5 of 7 in 2025-06-07 to 2025-09-18, with the only other member in Nov 2024) and near-zero in Dec-Mar.
The lost_mwh_reported_total (68.9 MWh) should be dominated by the single Emergency WO-2025-00521, with the reset-type tickets contributing little.
Other symptoms at Salt Fork Landing (inverter faults, surge/SPD replacements, ground faults) should also spike in the same June-September window.
Neighbouring sites in the same region should show comms_loss or surge-related work orders on or near 2025-06-07.
discriminating_evidence: Explicit environment tags: only 1 of 7 narratives mentions storm_or_lightning, and 6 are tagged 'none_mentioned' — weak support unless storm dates correlate with the untagged events too.
Off-season (winter) event count: any material winter comms_loss rate falsifies a purely storm-driven explanation.
Whether SPD/surge card replacements at this site cluster on the same dates as the reset-only tickets.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is partly a logging artifact: Salt Fork Landing raises a formal work order for trivial remote-clearable TCU dropouts (and its narratives show copy-paste templating and inconsistent coding), inflating the counted event rate relative to sites that clear the same dropouts without a ticket.
predictions: Near-verbatim narrative duplication should be detectable — WO-2025-00570 and WO-2025-00895 share almost identical wording from TECH-0110, as do WO-2025-00692 and WO-2025-00737.
Internal coding inconsistency: WO-2025-00895 is resolution_code RESET yet lists 'TCU board' in parts_used; several records carry uncertain=true with no root cause established.
Salt Fork comms_loss tickets should skew to P3/low labor_hours and near-zero reported lost MWh compared with comms_loss tickets fleet-wide.
A small number of techs (TECH-0110, TECH-0159, TECH-0222 cover all 7) should account for a disproportionate share of this site's comms_loss tickets relative to their share of total site work orders.
discriminating_evidence: Compare mean labor_hours and lost_mwh per comms_loss WO at this site vs fleet: materially lower values imply threshold/logging differences rather than worse hardware.
Check whether the site's elevated rate disappears when tickets under ~2 labor hours with RESET/NO-FAULT-FOUND codes are excluded.
Check whether the site's ticket-per-alarm ratio (if alarm counts are available) differs from peers, or whether a tech-level or shift-level handover changed the ticketing rate at a specific date.

verdict.reasoning: Seven comms_loss events against ~4.4 expected on 4.6 GW-months is a lift of 1.62 that does not survive Poisson scrutiny, and the member set is causally heterogeneous rather than a single failure mode: one lightning/surge-card emergency (WO-2025-00521), four bare TCU power-cycles with no fault stored (WO-2024-00276, WO-2025-00570, WO-2025-00698, WO-2025-00895) and two daisy-chain reseats (WO-2025-00692, WO-2025-00737). The strongest H1 evidence — reseating loose daisy-chain terminations — is matched almost verbatim in a control at a different site (Coralito Flats WO-2025-01128, 'TR-Z01 comm fault. Reseated daisy chain. Cleared.'), and no-fault-found tracker resets also appear at Two Rivers Crossing (WO-2025-00802) and Pine Hollow Station (WO-2025-00747), so the behaviour is fleet-normal, not Salt Fork-specific. Asset recurrence is thin: only TR-Z03 is noted as a repeat, and the other six members are on six distinct assets/zones spread across Z01, Z09, Z11, B03, B07 plus one site-level comms event, which is what H2 predicts and H1 does not. H3 is undermined because six of seven narratives are tagged 'none_mentioned' for environment and the November 2024 event sits outside storm season; H4 has some support (WO-2025-00895 is coded RESET yet lists a TCU board, and its narrative is near-identical to WO-2025-00570) but that is a coding hygiene issue, not a driver of the rate. Consumption is also trivial — five members under 3.5 hours with no parts — so even if real the impact would not justify a campaign.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Two members (WO-2025-00692, WO-2025-00737) resolve specifically by reseating daisy-chain connections at zone controllers, and WO-2025-00692 explicitly records a second visit to TR-Z03 within two months, which is the signature H1 predicts. If the next 3-6 months add further reseat-type events concentrated on the same zones, H1 would regain standing. Separately, WO-2025-00895 carries a TCU board under a RESET code, so parts consumption at this site may be understated in the aggregate.

population_at_risk.description: No distinct at-risk population established; the events span six different tracker assets plus one site-level comms failure with no shared defective component identified.
population_at_risk.basis: not quantifiable from this data

verdict.recommended_action: Take no remediation action; set a watch on Salt Fork Landing comms_loss and tracker-zone repeat visits (TR-Z03 in particular) and re-test the rate after another 3-6 GW-months of exposure, and correct the parts/resolution-code mismatch on WO-2025-00895.
verdict.business_headline: Salt Fork Landing's comms_loss rate is within normal variation for its small exposure base — the reset tickets look identical to comparable work at Coralito Flats, Two Rivers Crossing and Pine Hollow, so no commercial action is warranted.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is a taxonomy artifact: the extracted symptom 'cooling_airflow_low' collapses at least three causally unrelated failure modes (single seized fan in a six-fan bank, loaded/blocked air filters, and bird nests in the intake plenum), so no single CE-4000 defect exists and the aggregate lift is an artifact of one label absorbing more distinct causes on this model than on peers.
predictions: Splitting the 12 members by narrative-derived root cause gives roughly 5 seized-fan, 4 blocked-filter, 2 nest, 1 vendor-referred/unknown, and no single subgroup exceeds the 0.021 peer median rate on its own

The 'component' field is internally inconsistent with narrative text (e.g. WO-2025-00785 and WO-2025-01089 are coded cooling_fan but describe a nest and a filter change respectively), indicating extraction noise rather than a coherent failure population
Resolution codes are scattered across RESET, PART-REPL, CLEANED, NO-FAULT-FOUND and VENDOR-REFERRED with no dominant code, unlike a genuine single-defect cluster
No asset_id appears twice and every record has recurrence=false; a real component defect would produce at least some repeat visits on the same serials
Peer models, re-extracted with the same pipeline, show the same three causes but split across separate symptom labels (e.g. 'filter_blocked', 'fan_fault'), depressing their per-label rates
discriminating_evidence: Re-running the rate computation on the seized-fan subset alone against the peer seized-fan subset: if CE-4000 is still >1.5x lifted, H1 fails and H4 gains
A codebook/mapping review showing whether peer models have alternative symptom labels available that CE-4000 records do not
Presence of duplicated boilerplate text (WO-2024-00107 and WO-2024-00155 are near-verbatim identical, same tech) indicating template-driven narratives that inflate apparent homogeneity

hypotheses.statement: The elevation is ordinary sampling variation: 12 events against an expected ~6.9 at the peer median over a ~2-year window on 327 units is within Poisson noise for a small-count cluster, and no CE-4000-specific effect is present.
predictions: The Poisson/exact 95% confidence interval on 12 events over 327 unit-observations includes the peer median rate of 0.021
Year-by-year counts are unstable (roughly 2 in 2024, 6 in 2025, 3 in 2026) with no monotonic trend and each year's rate individually indistinguishable from peers
Several peer models with similarly small cohorts also show lifts in the 1.5-2.0 range for other symptoms, i.e. this lift is not an outlier among all candidate cells tested
Total impact is small and consistent with routine work: 63.2 labor hours across 12 jobs (~5.3 h mean) and 34 MWh reported lost, no P1-dominated severity profile (only 1 of 12 is P1)
discriminating_evidence: Multiple-comparison correction across all model x symptom cells: if the corrected significance vanishes, H2 is favoured over H1/H3/H4
Whether CE-4000 unit-years of exposure differ from peers (older fleet or longer observation window) — normalising by unit-years rather than unit count may erase the lift entirely
Comparing alarm-threshold/telemetry configuration: if CE-4000 raises cabinet-temp alarms at a lower setpoint, it generates more work orders at identical physical condition

hypotheses.statement: The events are driven by site and mounting-position conditions (dust ingress near access tracks, avian nesting, high ambient heat) rather than by the CE-4000 design, and CE-4000 units happen to be over-represented at dusty or bird-heavy sites.
predictions: The 12 events concentrate on a handful of sites (Hollowell Ranch, Almond Row, Cypress Landing, Blue Slate Ridge each appear 2x) rather than being uniform across all sites hosting CE-4000
Non-CE-4000 inverters at those same sites show an elevated cooling/filter work-order rate in the same periods
Filter and nest events cluster seasonally: nest findings in spring/early summer (2025-08, 2026-04) and filter blockages in the hot months, with few or none in winter
Environment tags and free text repeatedly cite dust, soiling, end-of-row/access-track position or high ambient (WO-2025-00346, WO-2026-00369) rather than component quality
Assets flagged sit disproportionately in perimeter/end-of-row positions if position metadata exists
discriminating_evidence: Site-stratified rate comparison: if CE-4000 lift disappears once compared only against peer models at the same sites, H3 is supported and H4 rejected
Whether the seized-fan events (which are not obviously environmental) are geographically spread while filter/nest events are site-concentrated
Preventive-maintenance record check: sites with shorter filter intervals should show no filter-driven corrective work orders

hypotheses.statement: CE-4000 cooling fans suffer premature bearing seizure, with individual fans in the six-fan bank failing well before design life, producing a genuine model-specific corrective load independent of filters or nesting.
predictions: The seized-fan subset alone (WO-2024-00107, WO-2024-00155, WO-2025-00404, WO-2025-01072, WO-2025-01089, WO-2025-00435) exceeds the peer per-unit fan-replacement rate
Failed units share a narrow commissioning-date or serial-block range (asset IDs cluster in the CES40-18xx / CES40-24xx blocks) consistent with a fan lot or date-code
Fan part consumption for CE-4000 exceeds forecast/PM issue rates in the spares data, and single-fan replacements recur on the same asset within 12-24 months
Narratives consistently report the remaining fans healthy at time of failure, i.e. random single-unit bearing failure rather than a bank-wide or control-board cause
Vendor involvement appears repeatedly (WO-2025-00404 VENDOR-REFERRED, WO-2025-00435 vendor diagnostics), suggesting an unresolved OEM-side issue
discriminating_evidence: Fan part numbers and manufacture date codes on replaced units: a shared lot supports H4; unrelated lots and long service ages support normal wear
Age-at-failure distribution versus rated fan life — failures concentrated well below rated hours discriminate defect from end-of-life wear
Whether any asset generates a second fan seizure; zero recurrence across 327 units over three years argues against a systemic defect and back toward H1/H2

verdict.reasoning: The 12 members are not one failure population: six are single seized fans in a six-fan bank (WO-2024-00107, WO-2024-00155, WO-2025-00404, WO-2025-00435, WO-2025-01072, WO-2025-01089), four are loaded/blocked air filters (WO-2025-00346, WO-2025-00716, WO-2026-00596, WO-2026-00669), and two are bird nests in the intake plenum (WO-2025-00785, WO-2026-00369) — three causally unrelated modes absorbed by one extracted label. Split by cause, no subgroup clears the 0.021 peer median on 327 units (6/327 = 0.018 fan, 4/327 = 0.012 filter, 2/327 = 0.006 nest), so the 1.76 lift exists only at the aggregate label level, which is the signature of H1 rather than H4. The component field is demonstrably unreliable — WO-2025-00785 (a bird nest) and WO-2025-01089/WO-2026-00369 are coded cooling_fan while narratives describe nests and filters — and resolution codes scatter across RESET, PART-REPL, CLEANED, NO-FAULT-FOUND and VENDOR-REFERRED, unlike a coherent defect cluster. The controls settle it: PM records on the same model and sites (WO-2025-00597, WO-2025-01056, WO-2025-00060) repeatedly find 'filters loaded, swapped, all six fans running,' i.e. the same physical condition is routine planned work on CE-4000, and whether it lands in this cluster depends on PM-versus-CM timing, not on a model defect. H2 is compatible with the data (12 events versus ~6.9 expected is within Poisson range) but H1 explains more of what is actually visible — the cause heterogeneity and the mis-coded component field — and no asset repeats and no recurrence flag is set anywhere, which argues directly against H4; H3 is only weakly supported since the seized-fan events are geographically spread across five sites.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: The seized-fan subgroup is the largest single mode (6 events) and two of those involved OEM diagnostics (WO-2025-00404 VENDOR-REFERRED, WO-2025-00435, 11.0 labor hours), so an unresolved vendor-side fan issue cannot be fully excluded from 12 records alone; a proper fan-only rate comparison against peer models would be needed to close that out. WO-2024-00107 and WO-2024-00155 are near-verbatim narratives from the same tech (TECH-0152), which could mask either template noise or two genuine identical fan failures. Small counts also mean low power to detect a modest real effect.

population_at_risk.description: No CE-4000-specific defect population identified; filter loading and single-fan replacement appear at comparable frequency in routine PM controls on the same model and sites.
population_at_risk.basis: Cause-split of the 12 members against the 327-unit cohort yields per-cause rates (0.018, 0.012, 0.006) all at or below the 0.021 peer median.

verdict.recommended_action: Send this back to the extraction/codebook owner to split 'cooling_airflow_low' into distinct labels (fan_fault, filter_blocked, intake_obstruction) and correct the component field mis-coding on WO-2025-00785, WO-2025-01089 and WO-2026-00369, then re-run the model-vs-peer rate comparison on the fan-fault subset alone before any commercial action.
verdict.business_headline: The CE-4000 cooling flag is a labelling artifact — three unrelated causes (seized fans, loaded filters, bird nests) totalling 63.2 labor hours across 12 jobs share one symptom code, and none of them individually exceeds the peer rate, so no warranty or campaign action is warranted.

hypotheses.statement: MG-3300 ground faults are ordinary background variation for the installed base: at 0.084/unit against a peer median of 0.080 (lift 1.05, 24 events over 287 units and ~2.5 years) this cluster carries no model-specific signal and would disappear under any resampling.
predictions: Peer models' ground_fault work orders contain the same narrative mix (chafed home run at rack upright, pinched connector at gland plate, megger-OK reset) at similar proportions.
The 24 events spread across sites roughly in proportion to MG-3300 unit counts per site, with no site exceeding its expected share by more than Poisson noise.
Mean labor hours (99.7/24 = 4.2 h) and lost MWh per event (~1.9) sit inside the interquartile range for ground_fault work orders on all other models.
Splitting the 24 events by year yields no monotonic trend; counts per year are consistent with a flat rate.
discriminating_evidence: A per-model Poisson/exact test showing p >> 0.05 for MG-3300 vs the pooled peer rate kills the systemic-defect readings.
If instead the events concentrate in a minority of assets or a single vintage prefix, the uniform-background story fails in favour of H2.

hypotheses.statement: The repair-confirmed subset is an installation-workmanship defect tied to specific build crews/combiner cans (home runs tied against rack steel, connectors trapped on the gland plate), not to the MG-3300 inverter design, so the events cluster by asset vintage and combiner ID rather than by model.
predictions: Ground_fault WOs with a physical finding concentrate in a subset of asset-ID vintage prefixes (e.g. MGX33-17xx/20xx vs 24xx) and in a handful of CB-Bxx cans rather than spreading evenly.
Repeat ground_fault WOs appear on other strings inside the same combiner can (CB-B04, CB-B08, etc.) within months of the first, matching the techs' 'check the other entries in this can' note.
Non-MG-3300 inverters sharing the same sites and install crews show the same chafe/pinch narratives at comparable rates.
PM work orders raised after these CMs at the same sites record additional found-and-corrected chafe points.
discriminating_evidence: Cross-tabulate finding type against site/crew/vintage: co-location with install cohort (and presence in non-MG-3300 models at those sites) supports H2 and rules out a model-inherent defect.
If the physical findings are uniformly scattered across all vintages and sites, H2 collapses back to H1.

hypotheses.statement: The 'walked the strings, meggered OK, reset held' subset (roughly half the sample) is nuisance GFDI tripping — a detection-threshold/firmware behaviour with no physical fault — and is being pooled with genuine insulation failures under one symptom label.
predictions: The NFF/reset subset separates cleanly on work-order fields: resolution_code in RESET/NO-FAULT-FOUND, parts_used empty or fuse-only, component 'none'/'string_inverter', extracted.uncertain = true.
Assets in the NFF subset show repeat ground_fault WOs over time (recurrence), whereas repair-confirmed assets do not recur after the fix.
NFF events cluster by calendar window (early morning / post-rain / winter dates) or by firmware revision noted in the narrative (e.g. 'rev 6.0.0'), while repair events do not.
Lost MWh per event is materially lower for the NFF subset than for the repair subset.
discriminating_evidence: Stratify the 24 events into NFF vs physical-finding and recompute rate per unit for each: if only the NFF stratum is elevated versus peers, the driver is detection behaviour, not hardware.
Check whether NFF events on MG-3300 correlate with a firmware revision field; correlation supports H3, absence pushes toward H1/H4.

hypotheses.statement: Apparent cluster coherence is inflated by logging practice — near-verbatim boilerplate narratives and resolution codes that contradict the narrative text (SW-UPDATE for a connector replacement, NO-FAULT-FOUND for an in-place repair, PART-REPL with empty parts field) — so the cluster reflects how these WOs were written, not what happened in the field.
predictions: High verbatim/near-duplicate n-gram overlap between narratives, including across different sites, techs and years (e.g. the identical 'Walked the strings, nothing obvious. Meggered ok, reset and it held' string).
Resolution_code disagrees with narrative-derived action in a large fraction of these 24 WOs, and at a similar rate on other models' WOs.
parts_used is empty on a substantial share of WOs coded PART-REPL, and fuses appear on WOs coded RESET.
A small number of techs (e.g. TECH-0138, TECH-0117, TECH-0051) author a disproportionate share of the cluster and of the duplicated wording.
discriminating_evidence: Compute code-vs-narrative mismatch and duplicate-text rates for MG-3300 ground_fault against a random sample of all WOs: comparable rates mean this is corpus-wide logging noise, not an MG-3300 pattern.
If duplicated wording is concentrated in a few tech IDs while the physical findings still segregate by combiner can, H4 explains the labelling but H2 still explains the underlying faults.

verdict.reasoning: The cluster rate (0.084/unit vs peer median 0.080, lift 1.05, 24 events over 287 units and ~2.5 years) carries no model-specific signal, and the narratives confirm it: the physical findings are the ordinary chafed-home-run and pinched-connector modes, scattered across nine sites (WO-2024-00084 Pecan Fork, WO-2024-00149 Birch Coulee, WO-2025-00120 Red Clay Flats, WO-2025-00497 Joshua Fork, WO-2026-00544 Sawgrass Reach) and across every vintage prefix from 16xx to 24xx (WO-2025-00120 MGX33-1646D, WO-2026-00050 MGX33-1744D, WO-2024-00351 MGX33-2011A, WO-2026-00142 MGX33-2408A). H2 predicted concentration by combiner can and vintage plus repeat faults inside the same can; instead the 15 identified cans (CB-B01-05, B02-10, B03-07, B03-14, B04-05, B05-18, B05-24, B07-01, B07-20, B08-06, B08-11, B08-17, B09-12, B09-14, B10-03) are each hit exactly once, which by H2's own discriminating test collapses it back to H1. The matched control WO-2026-00462 is a KVP36 unit at Blackfoot Draw with a verbatim-equivalent finding ('CB-B03-17, chafed home run on the rack'), showing the wear mode is fleet-wide and not MG-3300-attributable. H3 and H4 describe real texture — a large NFF/reset stratum (WO-2024-00037, WO-2024-00074, WO-2025-00587, WO-2026-00427) with copy-paste wording, and resolution codes that contradict the narrative (SW-UPDATE for a connector swap in WO-2025-00753, NO-FAULT-FOUND for an in-place repair in WO-2024-00344) — but the controls show the same sloppiness corpus-wide (SW-UPDATE on an inspection in WO-2025-00127, RESET on a bird-nest cleanout in WO-2025-00823, WO-2025-00677 'wrong site closing'), so neither is an MG-3300 pattern either.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Roughly two-thirds of the events have a genuine physical finding, and two techs explicitly flag install workmanship and recommend checking sibling entries in the same can (WO-2024-00084, WO-2024-00235). If a can-level inspection ever did turn up multiple bad entries per can, the uniform-background reading would weaken. Also, mean labor of ~4 h per event across 24 events is not nothing in aggregate, and one event ran 8.6 h (WO-2025-00587) — but that is dispatch cost on a fleet-typical fault rate, not a model defect.

population_at_risk.description: No elevated subpopulation identified. The MG-3300 fleet of 287 units experiences ground faults at the peer rate, and the same failure mode appears on non-MG-3300 hardware at shared sites.
population_at_risk.basis: Rate 0.084/unit vs peer median 0.080 (lift 1.05); findings distributed one-per-can across 15 distinct cans, 9 sites and all vintage prefixes, so no coherent at-risk cohort is derivable.

verdict.recommended_action: Close CAND-024 without a warranty or remediation campaign, and instead fold the two tech recommendations to inspect sibling home-run entries at CB-B04 and CB-B08 (WO-2024-00235, WO-2024-00084) into the existing routine cable-management PM scope.
verdict.business_headline: MG-3300 ground faults run at the fleet-wide rate (lift 1.05) and the same chafed-home-run findings appear on other inverter models at the same sites — no MG-3300 claim or campaign is warranted.

hypotheses.statement: The CE-4000 ground_fault cluster is ordinary variation: at 0.08 faults per unit against a peer median of 0.084 (lift 0.95), the CE-4000 fleet is faulting at or slightly below the rate of comparable models, and the 26 work orders are simply what a 327-unit installed base produces.
predictions: Ground-fault rate per unit for other inverter models in the same corpus falls in a band that comfortably contains 0.08; no peer model is dramatically lower.
The 26 work orders spread across many distinct asset_ids (near 26 unique units) rather than concentrating on a repeat-offender subset.
Labor hours per WO (mean ~4.7 h) and lost MWh per WO (~2.2) are within the same range as ground_fault WOs on peer models.
Arrival of the 26 WOs over the 2024-07 to 2026-06 window is roughly uniform after adjusting for fleet growth; no step change tied to a model revision or firmware release.
discriminating_evidence: Compute ground_fault rate per unit-year (not per unit) by model; if CE-4000 remains at or below peers once exposure time is normalised, the cluster is noise.
If instead the WOs concentrate in a handful of sites or serial ranges far above what a uniform-rate model predicts, H1 is falsified in favour of H2.
Compare CE-4000 ground_fault rate to CE-4000's own rate for other symptoms; if ground_fault is not elevated within-model either, there is nothing model-specific to explain.

hypotheses.statement: The real pattern is not model-level but a DC home-run routing and securement workmanship defect confined to specific combiner blocks and sites (chafing against rack steel, pinched connectors in CB-Bxx), which would appear on any inverter model wired by the same crews.
predictions: Ground-fault WOs concentrate disproportionately at a few sites (Kettle Run, Pine Hollow Station appear repeatedly in the sample) rather than spreading evenly across all sites hosting CE-4000.
Within those sites, the CB-B## identifiers cluster on a small number of blocks, with repeat WOs on the same or adjacent combiner boxes.
Non-CE-4000 inverters at the same sites show ground_fault WOs with the same narrative signature ('chafed home run', 'pinched connector') at a comparable or higher rate.
The 'chafed/pinched' subgroup resolves with repaired_in_place or part_replaced and shows a rising count with asset age at a given site, while free-text recurrence flags cluster on the same block.
Serial-year prefixes in asset_id (18xx, 19xx, 20xx, 24xx) span the whole range, i.e. the fault is not tied to a manufacturing vintage.
discriminating_evidence: Re-aggregate the same 26 WOs by site and by combiner-box ID; a strong site/block concentration with a flat model-level rate separates H2 from H1 and from any model-specific defect.
Query ground_fault WOs at the affected sites filtered to other inverter models: if they show the same chafe/pinch narratives, the cause is wiring workmanship, not the CE-4000.
Check whether the chafe/pinch WOs share installation contractor or commissioning date fields if present in the WO record.

hypotheses.statement: A distinct subgroup of these WOs are nuisance ground-fault alarms from inverter firmware rather than genuine insulation faults, evidenced by 'megger OK, reset held, nothing found' narratives, and should segregate by firmware version.
predictions: Roughly a third to a half of the 26 WOs carry resolution NO-FAULT-FOUND or RESET with action reset_or_restart and no parts consumed, and their narratives mention megger/insulation readings passing.
Firmware strings appearing in narratives (e.g. 4.3.0, 4.4.1) are non-randomly distributed: the reset-only subgroup concentrates on particular versions while the chafe/pinch subgroup does not.
The reset-only subgroup shows lower lost_mwh per WO and lower recurrence on the same asset than the chafe/pinch subgroup, or conversely repeats on the same asset without any physical repair.
Reset-only WOs are flagged uncertain=true far more often than the repair WOs (visible in the sample).
discriminating_evidence: Split the 26 WOs by resolution_code/action into 'physical repair' vs 'reset only' and compare firmware mentions, repeat-visit intervals per asset, and lost MWh; a clean firmware-version split supports H3 over both H1 and H2.
If reset-only events recur on the same asset_id after a firmware upgrade WO appears in the record, H3 is weakened; if they stop after the upgrade, H3 is supported.
Check whether reset-only events cluster in time (fleet-wide alarm storms on the same dates) rather than per-asset.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster's apparent coherence is partly a logging artifact: several narratives are near-verbatim duplicates and resolution_code frequently contradicts the narrative (NO-FAULT-FOUND on WOs where a connector was replaced, PART-REPL on WOs where only a reset was performed), so counts and structured fields cannot be trusted at face value.
predictions: Text-similarity comparison across the 26 narratives finds multiple pairs above a high similarity threshold, consistent with template or copy-paste entry by the same tech.

Cross-tabulating resolution_code against extracted.action yields a substantial mismatch rate (e.g. NO-FAULT-FOUND paired with part_replaced, PART-REPL paired with reset_or_restart), as seen in at least 5 of the 14 sampled WOs.

Some asset_ids appear more than once within a few days with near-identical narratives, indicating duplicate WOs for a single event rather than distinct failures (the 'second trip out here this week' note is a candidate).
Certain techs (e.g. TECH-0222, TECH-0063, TECH-0088) account for a disproportionate share of the 26 and reuse identical phrasing across sites.
discriminating_evidence: De-duplicate by (asset_id, symptom, 7-day window) and recount; if n drops materially below 26 the rate falls further below the peer median and the cluster dissolves.

Recompute the cluster using only narrative-derived labels, ignoring resolution_code; if the picture changes substantially, the structured fields are unreliable and any lift estimate built on them is suspect.
If duplicates and code mismatches are equally common in peer-model ground_fault WOs, this is a corpus-wide logging issue and does not explain anything specific to CE-4000.

verdict.reasoning: As posed this is a model-level claim, and the model-level signal is absent: 26 ground-fault WOs on 327 CE-4000 units is 0.08/unit against a peer median of 0.084 (lift 0.95), i.e. at or just below comparable models. The matched controls settle it — KVP36 inverters produce the identical narrative signatures at the same sites, with WO-2025-00004 ('pinched connector in CB-B05-08', Bitter Draw) reading as a near word-for-word twin of member WO-2024-00069 and WO-2025-00796, and WO-2026-00592 ('walked the strings... meggered ok, reset and it held') matching the reset-only members WO-2025-00044, WO-2025-00084, WO-2025-00919 and WO-2025-01071. H2's mechanism (DC home-run chafe and pinched connectors) is clearly real in the text, but it is cross-model wiring workmanship, not a CE-4000 attribute, so it does not validate this candidate; the only site with any real mass is Kettle Run (WO-2025-00548, WO-2025-00943, WO-2025-01268, WO-2026-00423), and without per-site unit counts that is not separable from chance. H4 is also partly right and further deflates the count: WO-2024-00185 and WO-2025-00645 are near-verbatim templates from the same tech at different sites (both ending 'that is the second one like it on this block'), and resolution_code contradicts the narrative repeatedly (WO-2024-00016 PART-REPL with no parts and a reset only; WO-2025-00069/WO-2025-01191/WO-2025-01268 pairing RESET or NO-FAULT-FOUND with a physical repair), so the structured fields cannot carry a lift argument. Nothing here is model-specific once normalised by installed base.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: The chafe/pinch subgroup is a genuine physical failure mode, not noise: at least nine members describe a home run worn through against rack steel or a pinched connector in a combiner (WO-2024-00185, WO-2025-00548, WO-2025-00645, WO-2025-00943, WO-2025-01191, WO-2025-01268, WO-2026-00423, WO-2026-00507, WO-2026-00656), Kettle Run alone contributes four of them, and two narratives assert a repeat on the same block. If site-level unit counts showed Kettle Run or a specific combiner block far above expectation, a site-scoped H2 finding could survive even though the CE-4000 framing does not.

population_at_risk.description: No excess population attributable to the CE-4000 model; its ground-fault rate sits at the peer median, and the same failure narratives appear on KVP36 units at the same sites.
population_at_risk.basis: rate_per_unit 0.08 vs peer_median_rate 0.084 across 327 installed CE-4000 units, corroborated by cross-model controls WO-2025-00004 and WO-2026-00592

verdict.recommended_action: Close this candidate as a model-attribution artifact and re-cut all ground-fault work orders by site and combiner-block ID across every inverter model, starting with Kettle Run and its CB-B03/B04/B06 blocks, before committing any inspection crew time.
verdict.business_headline: CE-4000 ground faults are running at the fleet norm, not above it — the chafed home runs show up on other inverter makes too, so this is a wiring-workmanship question to re-scope by site, not a CE-4000 problem.

hypotheses.statement: Caprock Mesa has a workmanship/cable-management defect in which combiner home runs were installed without standoffs and chafe through against rack steel under tracker motion and thermal cycling, producing genuine DC ground faults across multiple blocks.
predictions: A majority of Caprock Mesa ground_fault WOs with a definite root cause should carry extracted.component = 'conductor_or_connector' and narrative text naming a chafed/abraded home run at the rack, not module or inverter internals.

The faults should be spread over many distinct combiner IDs and blocks (B02, B03, B04, B06, B07 already present) rather than repeating on one asset, i.e. new-location recurrence rather than same-asset recurrence.
Repairs should be 'repaired_in_place' with low parts consumption (conductor repair, string connector) and modest labor (2-8 h), matching the observed 37.2 h / 9 WOs = 4.1 h mean.
Other sites sharing the same racking vendor / EPC / commissioning year should show a similarly elevated ground_fault rate; sites with different racking should sit near the 0.92 fleet rate.
Ground_fault WOs at this site should be under-represented in the first months after COD and increase with cumulative tracker cycles (rising counts per year 2024 -> 2026).
discriminating_evidence: Physical confirmation in narratives of insulation damage at a steel contact point in >=50% of cases separates this from moisture-only or noise explanations.
If recurrences land on NEW combiners each time, H1 is favoured; if they repeat on the same 2-3 combiners with clean connections, H1 is weakened in favour of H4.
Cross-site query: elevated rate at sibling sites with identical racking supports H1; isolation to Caprock Mesa alone weakens it.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is inflated by record-keeping artifacts: templated/copy-pasted narratives and the same physical fault being logged twice (once against the inverter asset, once against the downstream combiner), so the de-duplicated event count is materially below 9.
predictions: Near-identical narrative strings should be detectable: WO-2024-00063 and WO-2026-00536 are almost word-for-word ('home run chafed through on the rack ... Invertor back in service'), and WO-2026-00120 vs WO-2026-00290 differ only in block ID.

Some ground_fault WOs should pair an inverter asset_id (e.g. KVP36-1629C-0260) with a combiner asset_id (CB-B07-11) referenced inside the text, within a short date window, indicating one event logged on two asset keys.
After de-duplication by (asset-hierarchy, +/-7 day window, narrative similarity) the count should fall toward 5-7, dropping rate_per_gw_month to roughly 1.2-1.6 and lift below ~1.7.
Total lost_mwh_reported (24.4 MWh over 9 WOs) should be duplicated or zero on the paired records if the same outage is double-booked.
discriminating_evidence: Run string-similarity on the 9 narratives: high pairwise similarity plus shared labor-hour values indicates templating/duplication rather than nine independent field events.
Check the asset parent-child table: if the combiner named in an inverter-keyed WO also has its own WO within days, the events are duplicates.

If narratives are near-duplicates but asset IDs, dates and techs are all distinct and non-hierarchical, H2 is refuted and H1 survives (technicians reusing boilerplate for genuinely repeated failures).

hypotheses.statement: Nine ground_fault WOs over 4.3 GW-months is ordinary Poisson variation against a fleet expectation of ~4 events, made to look notable only by scanning many site-by-symptom cells.
predictions: The 95% Poisson interval on 9 events (~4.1 to 17.1 counts, i.e. ~0.95 to 4.0 per GW-month) should overlap the fleet rate of 0.92 at its lower bound, so the lift is not robust.
Splitting by year should show no sustained excess: e.g. 3 events in 2024, ~0 in 2025, 6 in 2026, with the 2025 gap inconsistent with a persistent site-level hazard.
Several other site|symptom cells in the same scan should show lift >= 2.0 at n < 12, consistent with multiple-comparison noise rather than one special site.

Caprock Mesa's rate for unrelated symptoms (arc_fault, string underperformance, tracker) should sit near fleet average; a site-wide reporting or exposure error would lift all symptoms, and a real defect would lift only related ones.
discriminating_evidence: Compute the exact Poisson tail and a false-discovery correction across all site|symptom cells; if adjusted significance disappears, H3 wins.
A 2025 gap of many months with zero ground_fault WOs at the site argues for noise; a steady 2024-2026 arrival rate argues against H3.
Verify exposure_gw_months is correctly derived (correct AC/DC capacity and in-service months); an understated denominator would fully explain the lift without any physical cause.

hypotheses.statement: A subset of the events are transient, moisture-driven ground faults (wetting of aged combiner/harness insulation) that clear on drying, evidenced by NO-FAULT-FOUND / megger-normal outcomes and repeat alarms on the same blocks with clean connections.
predictions: The recurring-outcome WOs (extracted.recurrence = true, e.g. B02, B04, B06, B07) should show resolution codes of NO-FAULT-FOUND, ADJUSTED, OTHER or VENDOR-REFERRED and actions of reset_or_restart / inspected_only, with no defective part identified.
Alarm dates should cluster seasonally or after precipitation-tagged WOs at the same site (2024 events all in July; 2026 events Feb-Jun), rather than being uniformly distributed.
Narratives should repeatedly report insulation-resistance ('meggered') readings that are normal or 'low side of normal' at the time of inspection, as in WO-2026-00598.
Repeat events should concentrate on the same block/combiner IDs (B07 appears at least three times) rather than migrating to new hardware.
discriminating_evidence: Join WO timestamps to site weather or to the environment field of other same-day WOs: rain/high-humidity tagging on the transient cases separates H4 from H1's mechanical chafe.
Compare quantitative megger values on repeat blocks over time: a downward trend indicates progressive insulation degradation (H4), stable normal values indicate an intermittent mechanical short (H1).

If every recurring case is on a block that also had a confirmed chafe repair, H4 collapses into H1; if recurring blocks have no confirmed chafe finding at all, the two mechanisms are genuinely distinct.

verdict.reasoning: The site-level lift is not robust once the controls are read: the exact 'home run chafed through against the rack' repair (WO-2024-00002, WO-2024-00063, WO-2026-00536) appears verbatim at Northfield Bend (WO-2025-00373) and the closely related 'pinched connector in CB-...' repair appears at Pine Hollow Station (WO-2025-00158) and Northfield Bend (WO-2026-00229), so the chafe/connector mechanism is a fleet-general DC-side wear pattern, not a Caprock-specific workmanship defect — H1 fails its own cross-site prediction. H2 also fails: the near-identical narratives are templating, but the pairs are on distinct assets, blocks, techs and dates up to two years apart (WO-2024-00063 vs WO-2026-00536; WO-2026-00120 vs WO-2026-00290), so they are not double-booked single events. H3 largely holds — 9 events against ~4 expected on 4.3 GW-months, with a full-year gap in 2025 (the only 2025 Caprock records shown are PM/inspection, WO-2025-01110 and WO-2025-00161) — but it does not explain one thing the controls lack: four WOs coded recurring with clean connections and no defective part found (WO-2026-00120, WO-2026-00290, WO-2026-00558, WO-2026-00598), including a tech escalation with megger readings on the 'low side of normal'. That residual sub-pattern is consistent with progressive/moisture-driven insulation degradation on a handful of blocks (H4), but it is four work orders and roughly 12 labor hours, with no confirmed hardware failure, so it is real and worth a cheap look rather than a commercial claim.
verdict.contradicting_evidence: Three Caprock cases were confirmed physical chafe repairs with a definite root cause (WO-2024-00002, WO-2024-00063, WO-2026-00536), which would support a workmanship story if sibling-site controls did not show the identical repair (WO-2025-00373). Data hygiene is weak: WO-2026-00598 is keyed to asset CB-B06-22 while its narrative describes B07, and several narratives are boilerplate, so block-level counts are uncertain. Counts are also small enough that the 2026 run could be arrival-time clustering rather than a hazard.

population_at_risk.description: Four Caprock Mesa combiner blocks with unresolved repeat ground-fault activity and clean connections: B02, B04, B06 and B07 (B07 named repeatedly).
population_at_risk.basis: Distinct block IDs appearing in the four cluster members coded outcome='recurring' (WO-2026-00120 B04, WO-2026-00290 B02, WO-2026-00558 B07, WO-2026-00598 B06/B07 per narrative). Block-to-string counts are not in this data, so no MWh or unit-level exposure can be derived.

verdict.recommended_action: At the next scheduled Caprock Mesa PM, run and record quantitative insulation-resistance readings on all strings in blocks B02, B04, B06 and B07 and trend them against the 'low side of normal' values noted in WO-2026-00598, and fix the asset-ID/block mismatch in WO-2026-00598 so recurrence can be tracked per block.
verdict.business_headline: Caprock Mesa's ground-fault rate looks elevated mainly because a common fleet-wide chafe/connector failure mode is being logged there in bursts, but four blocks have repeat faults with no fault found and softening insulation readings that merit a one-shift megger survey rather than a site-wide campaign.

hypotheses.statement: The cluster is a dispatch/logging artifact: MG-3300 sites automatically generate a P2/P3 corrective work order for every self-clearing ride-through alarm, so MG-3300 shows more WOs than peers without experiencing more grid events.
predictions: Nearly all 8 members close with no parts, no action codes (NO-FAULT-FOUND / RESET / OTHER) and narratives stating the unit self-cleared before arrival — already true in 8/8 of the sample.
At the same sites, non-MG-3300 inverters should have alarm/event records for the same timestamps that either have no work order at all or are closed as informational/PM rather than CM.
Labor hours per WO should be dominated by travel/verification (1.5–6 h, no repair time) and lost_mwh per event should be small and roughly equal (~2 MWh) across all members.
The elevated MG-3300 rate should be present only in the CM-with-no-parts subset; if WOs with parts or downtime >1 shift are counted, the lift should collapse toward peer median.
discriminating_evidence: Compare per-event SCADA/alarm counts (not work-order counts) between MG-3300 and peer models: equal alarm rates with unequal WO rates confirms this and refutes a real defect.
Check whether MG-3300 sites share a CMMS auto-ticketing rule or alarm-forwarding configuration absent at peer-model sites.

hypotheses.statement: This is ordinary Poisson variation plus multiple-comparison selection: 8 events across 287 units over ~2 years is statistically indistinguishable from the peer rate once the number of model×symptom pairs screened is accounted for.
predictions: Events are dispersed across ≥6 distinct sites and ≥5 distinct months with no site or date accounting for more than ~2 events — the sample shows 7 sites and dates spanning 2024-07 to 2026-04.
Recomputing the rate per unit-year rather than per unit should narrow the lift, especially if MG-3300 units have longer average in-service exposure than the peer fleet.
No single MG-3300 asset_id should appear twice; recurrence flags should be site-level ('second one this month at this site'), not asset-level.
Other model×symptom pairs in the same corpus with n≈8 should show comparable lifts, i.e. this candidate is not an outlier among candidates.
discriminating_evidence: Exact Poisson test against the peer rate with a false-discovery correction across all screened candidates: if the corrected p-value is non-significant, prefer this over a defect hypothesis.
Repeat asset_ids or a rate that stays 3x elevated after exposure normalisation and FDR correction would refute this.

hypotheses.statement: MG-3300 firmware/LVRT settings are more conservative than peer inverters, so MG-3300 units trip offline on shallow (~180 ms, two-phase) transmission dips that co-located peer-model inverters ride through.
predictions: At mixed-fleet sites, for a given timestamped grid disturbance there should be MG-3300 ride-through WOs but no corresponding WOs or trip events on non-MG-3300 units at the same site.

Event records captured in narratives should consistently show voltage dips that are shallow/short (the Red Clay Flats WO logged ~180 ms undervoltage), i.e. near the ride-through threshold rather than deep faults.

The rate should be uniform across all MG-3300 units regardless of site, and should shift (up or down) at a common date if a firmware revision is applied — check WOs before/after any firmware/setting-change PM records.
Resolution codes should trend toward VENDOR-REFERRED over time as techs escalate (one such WO already present).
discriminating_evidence: Same-site, same-timestamp comparison of MG-3300 vs peer-model trip records is the cleanest separator from H1, H2 and H4.
Firmware/serial-block stratification: if events concentrate in one hardware or firmware revision block of the 287 units, this supports a defect; uniform spread across all revisions weakens it.

hypotheses.statement: The events are genuine external transmission-side disturbances, and MG-3300 units are over-represented only because that model is concentrated at sites on weak or fault-prone interconnections (site confounding, not model defect).
predictions: MG-3300 ride-through WOs should cluster by site/substation, with some sites contributing repeat events ('second one of these this month at this site' at Frostline Prairie) while other MG-3300 sites contribute zero.
At the affected sites, all inverters of every model — not just MG-3300 — should show ride-through or offline WOs on or near the same dates.
Dates should coincide across multiple assets within a site rather than being isolated single-asset events; check for same-day multi-asset WO bursts.
Normalising rate by site rather than by model should eliminate the MG-3300 lift; peer models installed at the same sites should show comparable per-unit rates.
discriminating_evidence: Site-stratified rate comparison: if MG-3300 units at a given site have the same ride-through WO rate as peer-model units at that same site, this hypothesis wins over H3.
Presence of same-date ride-through WOs on non-MG-3300 assets at Birch Coulee, Blackfoot Draw or Frostline Prairie would confirm a shared external cause.

verdict.reasoning: All eight members close with no repair: 8/8 narratives state the unit self-cleared and resynchronised before the tech arrived, output verified normal against neighbours, and resolution codes are NO-FAULT-FOUND/RESET/OTHER/VENDOR-REFERRED with no meaningful parts consumption (WO-2024-00038, WO-2024-00223, WO-2024-00285, WO-2025-01019, WO-2025-01190, WO-2026-00344, WO-2026-00361). The one member with an event record (WO-2024-00223) documents a ~180 ms two-phase undervoltage — a transmission-side disturbance, not a plant or inverter fault. The matched controls show the same physical phenomenon occurring at the same sites but coded under a different symptom label: WO-2025-01212 (an MG-3300 unit at Blackfoot Draw) and WO-2025-00770 (peer model KVP36 at Frostline Prairie) are both AC undervoltage trips with normal POI, closed with a reset. That label-boundary overlap means the MG-3300 'grid_ride_through' count is a ticketing/classification artifact rather than evidence of a model-specific ride-through weakness, which beats H3 (no evidence of MG-3300-only tripping — a peer KVP36 tripped on the same class of event) and is more explanatory than H2 alone, since a pure-chance story would not predict the systematic symptom-label split. Events are also spread over 7 sites, 8 distinct assets and 21 months with no asset repeating, so there is no defect population to act on.

Three different technicians (TECH-0072, TECH-0117, TECH-0044) independently attribute the breakage to rock thrown off the mower deck (WO-2024-00172, WO-2024-00175, WO-2024-00237, WO-2025-00220), and WO-2024-00175 gives the discriminating physical signature H1 predicts: impact points on the lower third with glass starred outward, plus the statement that this is the fourth such incident and that specified deck deflectors were never fitted. verdict.business_headline: Twenty-five modules at Caprock Mesa have been broken across four separate mower rock-strike incidents because contractually specified mower deck deflectors were never fitted — a preventable, recurring loss with an open technician recommendation unactioned since September 2024.
